period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
site: Alexandria (centre: Kom el-Dikka, the Eastern Harbour, Kom el-Shuqafa), Alexandria Governorate
nome: none (polis outside the nomes; its chora included the Mareotes)
greek_from_text: founded by Alexander the Great, early 331 BC (Arr. Anab. 3.1.5-3.2.2; Plut. Alex. 26; the Alexander Romance 1.32 gives the day as 25 Tybi); laid out by Deinokrates; capital of the Ptolemies from c. 313 BC
until_text: Administration: 'Amr ibn al-'As took the city by the treaty signed by the patriarch Cyrus (November 641); the Roman garrison and many Greek-speaking residents sailed away in September 642; after Manuel's reoccupation (645/646) 'Amr retook it by storm and razed its walls (646). Arabic replaced Greek in the government registers in 705/706 (order of the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik, al-Kindi). Speech: a Chalcedonian (Melkite) community stayed, the part of the population most likely to keep Greek; its see was vacant for most of c. 650-727 and was restored under Cosmas I (c. 727-768), whose church was again in communion with the Greek-speaking patriarchates (Theophanes, under 742/743). No dated Greek letter, contract or epitaph of an Alexandrian resident is known after the 7th c. By the 10th c. the Melkites of Egypt wrote Arabic: Patriarch Eutychius (Sa'id ibn Bitriq, born in Fustat 877, patriarch 933-940) wrote his Annals in Arabic and seems not to have known Greek. Greek remained the Melkite liturgical language, which does not extend the phase. The end of Greek speech is therefore placed c. 850 (750-950), later than the Egypt-wide estimate because of the Melkite community of the capital. Greek merchants and clergy from the empire in later centuries are newcomers.
fade_evidence: Emigration under the treaty of 641/642; Greek administration in Egypt to 705/706, with Greek-Arabic protocols and Greek fiscal documents into the 8th c.; Melkite see vacant c. 650-727, restored under Cosmas I (c. 727-768); Theophanes records the Alexandrian church's union with the other Chalcedonian patriarchates in 742/743; Melkite historiography in Arabic by the 10th c. (Eutychius, born 877, patriarch 933-940, who used Greek works only in translation); Greek kept as a liturgical language; Coptic and Arabic replaced Greek among the rest of the population.
ended_by: Taken by 'Amr ibn al-'As, 641 (treaty with the patriarch Cyrus), evacuated by the Roman army 642; stormed again by 'Amr after Manuel's revolt, 646, walls razed. Afterwards the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers kept in Arabic from 705/706 (al-Kindi), which ended Greek in government but was not a ban on speech; no act against Greek speech is recorded: the evidence shows emigration and a shift of the remaining Melkites to Arabic by the 10th c. Earlier blows: Ptolemy VIII's expulsion of scholars and massacres (145 BC and after); Caracalla's massacre of the youth (215, Cass. Dio 78.22-23); Aurelian's destruction of the Brucheion (272, after Zenobia's occupation and the revolt of Firmus); Diocletian's siege and sack after the revolt of Domitius Domitianus and Achilleus (297/298); the Persian conquest under Shahrbaraz (619).
founder: Alexander the Great (architect Deinokrates of Rhodes)
pre_greek_note: Strabo 17.1.6 says Rhakotis was an earlier Egyptian village on the site; the Egyptian Rꜥ-qd(.t) is first attested on the Satrap Stele (311 BC) and in Demotic, and Chauveau argued it meant 'building site', i.e. the new city itself, so a pre-Greek village of this name is disputed; harbour cores show human activity on the coast before 331 BC
status_evidence: royal foundation and Ptolemaic capital; polis with citizen tribes and demes, gymnasium and ephebes; boule restored by Septimius Severus (200/201); patriarchal see; Hierocles and Georgius Cyprius (capital of Aegyptus)
note: A large Greek-speaking Jewish community lived here from the 3rd c. BC (the Septuagint, Philo): attacked in the riots of 38 under the prefect Flaccus and in 66 (troops of Tiberius Julius Alexander), destroyed in the revolt of 115-117 (suppressed by Marcius Turbo under Trajan), revived, and expelled by the patriarch Cyril in 414/415 (Socrates, HE 7.13); Egyptian-speaking residents lived beside the Greek citizens throughout.

refoundations: Nikopolis, Octavian's foundation of 30 BC east of the city: separate entry

period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
other_names: Kanobos (Greek variant); Abu Qir (Arabic, from Abba Kyros, St Cyrus)
site: Abu Qir, Alexandria Governorate (partly submerged in Abu Qir Bay)
greek_from_text: Greek shipping used the Canopic mouth from the 6th c. BC (Hdt. 2.113, 2.179); the town flourished under the early Ptolemies (temples of Osiris and Sarapis; Canopus Decree, 238 BC)
until_text: Administration ended with 'Amr ibn al-'As's conquest (641/642). Speech: Greek-speaking pilgrims and residents are attested at the shrine of Cyrus and John at Menouthis to the 620s; after the conquest the town shrank to the village of Abu Qir and no Greek evidence is known. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Sophronius, Miracles of Cyrus and John (c. 610-620); the Serapeum replaced by the Pachomian monastery of Metanoia after 391; no Greek inscriptions after the 7th c. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
ended_by: No named act ended Greek speech; the town was taken with the Alexandrian region by 'Amr ibn al-'As (641/642). Earlier: the Serapeum of Kanopos destroyed under the patriarch Theophilus (391/392); the Isis shrine of Menouthis destroyed under Peter Mongos (c. 489). Under Arab rule the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers kept in Arabic from 705/706 (al-Kindi); this ended Greek as the language of government, and no ban on Greek speech is recorded.
pre_greek_note: Demotic pr-gwṭ (Peguat), with hieroglyphic variants, is attested only in Ptolemaic texts (305-30 BC), so whether it is an older Egyptian name or a rendering of the Greek one is uncertain; an Egyptian temple town and harbour existed before the Ptolemies.
bilingual_evidence: Egyptian temple town (Osiris, Sarapis) whose priests issued the Canopus Decree of 238 BC in hieroglyphic, Demotic and Greek; Greek resort town described by Strabo; Greek dedications of Ptolemy III; Greek-speaking pilgrims and residents in Sophronius' Miracles of Cyrus and John (7th c.)
status_evidence: Strabo 17.1.17 (polis); Canopus Decree (OGIS 56, 238 BC); main town of the Menelaite district; no bishop of Kanopos itself is attested
note: Strabo 17.1.18 names a separate city of Menelaos near Kanopos, which gave the Menelaite nome its name; the late Roman see of the Menelaites is linked with Schedia in the episcopal lists (separate entry). The emporion of Thonis-Herakleion nearby is listed among the rejected places.
sources: Strabo 17.1.17-18; Hdt. 2.113, 2.179; OGIS 56; Goddio & Fabre (eds.), Egypt's Sunken Treasures (2008); Sophronius, Miracles of Cyrus and John

until_text: Administration: Roman rule ended with the conquest of the Delta by 'Amr ibn al-'As (640-642); Greek remained the language of the tax registers until 705/706, when the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik ordered them kept in Arabic (al-Kindi). Speech: the Greek-speaking civic elite shrank by emigration (the treaty of 641 let Romans leave) and assimilation. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: No town-specific evidence after 641 (papyri rarely survive in the wet Delta); later bishops of the see belong to the Coptic church and wrote Coptic, then Arabic. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
ended_by: No named act ended Greek speech; the army of 'Amr ibn al-'As passed and fought here on its march on Alexandria (641). Under Arab rule the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers kept in Arabic from 705/706 (al-Kindi); this ended Greek as the language of government, and no ban on Greek speech is recorded.
pre_greek_note: 'Domain of Renenutet'; cemeteries from the Old Kingdom on.
bilingual_evidence: hundreds of funerary stelae of residents with Greek epitaphs (some Demotic), 1st-4th c. AD; Ptolemaic temples of Hathor and Apollo; bishops from 404
status_evidence: see: Arsinthios 404, Eulogios at Ephesus 431, Ioannes 689, Petros c. 743 (Worp); Greek stelae (Hooper 1961; Abd el-Al et al. 1985)
note: Before late antiquity Terenouthis was a large village rather than a city; it is included because it became a see and its residents wrote Greek epitaphs.
sources: Hooper, Funerary Stelae from Kom Abou Billou (1961); Worp, ZPE 100 (1994); Wikipedia: Terenuthis; Timm, Das christlich-koptische Ägypten

site: Sakha, Kafr el-Sheikh district, Kafr el-Sheikh Governorate
greek_from_text: nome metropolis under Rome: the Greek-speaking metropolite and gymnasial class was registered in every metropolis from AD 4/5 (boule from 200/201); no earlier town-specific Greek evidence found; metropolis of the Xoite nome (Strabo 17.1.19; Ptolemy 4.5); see from before 347 to c. 700; Hierocles
until_text: Administration: Roman rule ended with the conquest of the Delta by 'Amr ibn al-'As (640-642); Greek remained the language of the tax registers until 705/706, when the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik ordered them kept in Arabic (al-Kindi). Speech: the Greek-speaking civic elite shrank by emigration (the treaty of 641 let Romans leave) and assimilation. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: No town-specific evidence after 641 (papyri rarely survive in the wet Delta); later bishops of the see belong to the Coptic church and wrote Coptic, then Arabic. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
ended_by: No named act ended Greek speech. The Persians under Shahrbaraz held Egypt 619-629; 'Amr ibn al-'As conquered the Delta (640-642), and under his treaty with the patriarch Cyrus (November 641) Roman troops and Greek-speaking residents who wished to could leave (they sailed in September 642); the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers kept in Arabic from 705/706 (al-Kindi). No ban on Greek speech is recorded: the evidence shows emigration and a slow shift to Coptic and then Arabic.
pre_greek_note: Egyptian Ḫ3sww, capital of the 6th Lower Egyptian nome; Manetho's 14th Dynasty is 'Xoite'.
bilingual_evidence: metropolis of the Xoite nome (Strabo 17.1.19; Ptolemy 4.5); Roman nome coins; bishops from before 347 to c. 700 (Makedonios at Ephesus 431)
status_evidence: metropolis of the Xoite nome (Strabo 17.1.19; Ptolemy 4.5); see from before 347 to c. 700; Hierocles
sources: Strabo 17.1.19; Ptolemy 4.5; Worp, ZPE 100 (1994); Timm, Das christlich-koptische Ägypten

period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
site: Tell Atrib, Benha, Qalyubia Governorate
greek_from_text: Ptolemaic Greek town quarter, baths and workshops of the 3rd c. BC (Mysliwiec's Polish-Egyptian excavations at Tell Atrib); Greek dedication of a prayer-house by 'the Jews in Athribis' with Ptolemaios son of Epikydes, chief of police, for a Ptolemy and Cleopatra, 2nd c. BC (OGIS 96 = CIJ II 1443 = Horbury & Noy, JIGRE 27)
until_text: Administration Roman to 641 (John of Nikiu describes the Arab advance through the Athribite district), then Arab. Speech: Greek civic class not attested after the 7th c.; the Coptic see continued. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Bishops of Athribis in late antiquity and Coptic bishops later. Papyri rarely survive in the wet Delta, so private Greek documents of residents are few. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
ended_by: No named act ended Greek; the town fell to 'Amr ibn al-'As in the Delta campaign of 641 (John of Nikiu). Under Arab rule the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers kept in Arabic from 705/706 (al-Kindi); this ended Greek as the language of government, and no ban on Greek speech is recorded.
bilingual_evidence: Ptolemaic town with baths, villas and workshops making Greek-style pottery and terracottas (Polish excavations); Greek dedications of the Jewish prayer-house by the Jews of Athribis (Ptolemaic, JIGRE 27-28); Roman baths; Ammianus (22.16.6) names it among the great towns of Egypt; see
status_evidence: metropolis of the Athribite nome; nome coins; Amm. Marc. 22.16.6; see; Hierocles 728 (Augustamnica II)
sources: Amm. Marc. 22.16.6; Mysliwiec, Tell Atrib 1985-1995; John of Nikiu, Chronicle; Wikipedia: Athribis

period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
site: Tell Basta, on the edge of Zagazig, Sharqia Governorate
greek_from_text: Ptolemaic Greek inscriptions and Greek administration of the Boubastite nome, 3rd c. BC
until_text: Administration Roman to 641, then Arab. Speech: Greek civic class not attested after the 7th c.; the town declined. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Bishops Harpocration (Melitian, 325), Hermon (c. 340), Julianus (449); Coptic bishops of Basta in 1078 and 1102. Papyri rarely survive in the wet Delta, so private Greek documents of residents are few. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
ended_by: No named act: the treaty of Alexandria between the patriarch Cyrus and 'Amr ibn al-'As (November 641) handed Egypt to the Arabs; the Roman troops and many Greek-speaking officials and landowners left by September 642. Under Arab rule the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers kept in Arabic from 705/706 (al-Kindi); this ended Greek as the language of government, and no ban on Greek speech is recorded.
bilingual_evidence: Ptolemaic Greek inscriptions (a copy of the Canopus decree, 238 BC, was found here in 2004); metropolis of the Boubastite nome; see (Harpocration 325, Hermon c. 340, Julianus at Ephesus 449)
status_evidence: metropolis of the Boubastite nome (Hdt. 2.59, 2.137; Strabo 17.1.27); nome coins; see; Hierocles 728
note: The Greek inscriptions of the Ptolemaic period are official (priestly decree); the civic class is presumed from metropolis status.
sources: Hdt. 2.137-138; Strabo 17.1.27; Hierocles 728; Wikipedia: Bubastis

site: Abusir Bana, near Samannud, Gharbia Governorate
greek_from_text: metropolis of the Busirite nome under Rome (Strabo 17.1.19); gymnasial order of the metropoleis from AD 4/5; boule from 200/201
until_text: Administration Roman to 641, then Arab. Speech: no evidence of Greek speakers after late antiquity; the village continued as Coptic and then Arabic. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Bishops Hermaeon and Athanasius (449); non-Chalcedonian (Coptic) bishops from the 8th c. Papyri rarely survive in the wet Delta, so private Greek documents of residents are few. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
ended_by: No named act: the treaty of Alexandria between the patriarch Cyrus and 'Amr ibn al-'As (November 641) handed Egypt to the Arabs; the Roman troops and many Greek-speaking officials and landowners left by September 642. Under Arab rule the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers kept in Arabic from 705/706 (al-Kindi); this ended Greek as the language of government, and no ban on Greek speech is recorded.
bilingual_evidence: metropolis of the Busirite nome; Roman nome coins; see with bishops Hermaeon and Athanasius at Ephesus 449
status_evidence: metropolis of the Busirite nome (Hdt. 2.59; Strabo 17.1.19); nome coins under Hadrian; Hierocles (Aegyptus I); see (bishops at Ephesus 449)
note: Little excavated; the Greek-speaking civic class is inferred from the metropolis status.
sources: Hdt. 2.59, 2.61; Strabo 17.1.19; Wikipedia: Busiris (Lower Egypt)

period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
site: Ras el-Qasrun (El-Qals), on the spit of the Bardawil lagoon, North Sinai Governorate
greek_from_text: town at the sanctuary of Zeus Kasios where Pompey was buried, 48 BC (Strabo 16.2.33; Plutarch, Pompey 80); Hadrian restored the tomb, 130
until_text: Bishop Lampetius (431), correspondent of Isidore of Pelusium; listed by Hierocles and Georgius Cyprius; the town lay on the coast road taken by the Arabs in 639/640 and later disappeared at an unknown date. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850). Here the townspeople went over to Arabic.
fade_evidence: Isidore of Pelusium's Greek letters to bishop Lampetius (early 5th c.); Lampetius at Ephesus 431; listed by Hierocles and Georgius Cyprius. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
ended_by: No named act ended Greek speech. The coast road fell to the Arabs when 'Amr ibn al-'As marched from Palestine on Pelusium, winter 639/640 (Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam); the towns of the coast declined thereafter. Under Arab rule the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers kept in Arabic from 705/706 (al-Kindi); this ended Greek as the language of government, and no ban on Greek speech is recorded.
status_evidence: Hierocles 727; Georgius Cyprius; see (Lampetius at Ephesus 431)
note: The cult of Zeus Kasios came from the Syrian coast; the population was probably mixed (Greek, Egyptian, Arab).
sources: Strabo 16.2.32-33; Plutarch, Pompey 80; Hierocles 727; Catholic Encyclopedia: Casium

site: Tell el-Balamun, north of Shirbin, Dakahlia Governorate
greek_from_text: nome metropolis in the Roman period (Strabo 17.1.19; Ptolemy); gymnasial order of the metropoleis from AD 4/5
until_text: The town was occupied, with a paved Roman road, until about the 6th c. AD, then abandoned; the end of Greek speech there is not documented.
fade_evidence: Spencer's excavations (British Museum) show occupation into the 6th c. AD.
ended_by: No named act: the town was abandoned after the 6th c.
pre_greek_note: Paiuenamun ('island of Amun'), attested from the New Kingdom, survives in the modern name Tell el-Balamun.
bilingual_evidence: metropolis of the Lower Diospolite nome (Strabo, Ptolemy); Ptolemaic and Roman town on the tell
status_evidence: metropolis of the Diospolite nome of the Delta (Strabo 17.1.19); Hierocles (Aegyptus I: Diospolis)
note: Identification of Diospolis Kato with Tell el-Balamun is the usual one (Spencer).
sources: Strabo 17.1.19; Spencer, Excavations at Tell el-Balamun (1996-2003); Wikipedia: Tell el-Balamun

site: near Mahammediya, east of Pelusium, on the coast road, North Sinai Governorate
greek_from_text: fort and road town between Pelusium and Kasion (Strabo 16.2.33); first attested as a see c. 400, when Theophilus of Alexandria sought to make the hermit Nilammon its bishop (Sozomen 8.19)
until_text: Bishops to 451 (Stephen at Chalcedon); the town lay on the coast road taken by the Arabs in 639/640 and was later abandoned to sand and marsh at an unknown date. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850). Here the townspeople went over to Arabic.
fade_evidence: Bishops Eudaemon, Pirosus (late 4th-early 5th c.), Stephen (451); no later evidence. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
ended_by: No named act ended Greek speech. The coast road fell to the Arabs when 'Amr ibn al-'As marched from Palestine on Pelusium, winter 639/640 (Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam); the towns of the coast declined thereafter. status_evidence: Hierocles 727 (Gerrha and the two Skenai); see (Stephen at Chalcedon 451; Sozomen 8.19)
note: Called a Greek city because the coastal road towns had no Egyptian civic base; the language of its residents is not directly attested, and Arab and Egyptian residents are likely.
sources: Strabo 16.2.33; Sozomen, HE 8.19; Hierocles 727; Catholic Encyclopedia: Gerrha

site: Tell Hisn, El-Matariya, Cairo Governorate
greek_from_text: metropolis of the Heliopolite nome under Rome; gymnasial order of the metropoleis from AD 4/5; boule from 200/201
until_text: Administration: the Romans under Theodore lost the battle of Heliopolis to 'Amr ibn al-'As (July 640), and the district passed to the Arabs. Speech: the old town was small already in Strabo's day; no Greek evidence after the 7th c., and its stones were later carried off to build Cairo. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Strabo 17.1.29 found the town largely deserted; bishops of Heliopolis in the 4th-7th c. Papyri rarely survive in the wet Delta, so private Greek documents of residents are few. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
ended_by: Battle of Heliopolis: 'Amr ibn al-'As defeated the Roman army under Theodore, July 640 (John of Nikiu; Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam); no named act ended Greek speech. Under Arab rule the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers kept in Arabic from 705/706 (al-Kindi); this ended Greek as the language of government, and no ban on Greek speech is recorded.
bilingual_evidence: metropolis of the Heliopolite nome; Greek visitors and scholars (Strabo was shown the houses of Plato and Eudoxus); see; Hierocles
status_evidence: metropolis of the Heliopolite nome; nome coins; see; Hierocles 728
note: The Roman-period Greek community is poorly documented; entered as a nome capital and see.
sources: Strabo 17.1.27-29; Hierocles 728; Raue, Heliopolis und das Haus des Re (1999); Wikipedia: Heliopolis (ancient Egypt)

bilingual_evidence: city in Hierocles and Georgius Cyprius; bishop John at the councils of Ephesus 431 and 449
status_evidence: Hierocles 727; Georgius Cyprius; see suffragan of Pelusium (Le Quien)
note: Egyptian name and site unknown; the Greek evidence is only that of its clergy.
sources: Hierocles 727; Le Quien, Oriens Christianus II; Wikipedia: Hephaestus, Egypt

site: Tell Belim, between San el-Hagar and Tell el-Farama, Sharqia Governorate
greek_from_text: metropolis of the Sethroite nome in the Roman period (Strabo 17.1.24; Ptolemy 4.5.53); gymnasial order of the metropoleis from AD 4/5
until_text: Administration Roman to 639/640, then Arab. Speech: no evidence after the 6th c.; the town vanished in the Middle Ages. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).

bilingual_evidence: metropolis of the Sethroite nome under Rome, with the Greek-speaking gymnasial class of the metropoleis; city in Hierocles
status_evidence: metropolis of the Sethroite nome (Strabo 17.1.24; Ptolemy); nome coins under Hadrian; Hierocles 726; later a titular see

period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
site: Tell el-Maskhuta, Wadi Tumilat, Ismailia Governorate
greek_from_text: Ptolemaic canal town after Ptolemy II's works (Pithom stele, c. 264 BC); Heroonpolis in the Septuagint (Gen. 46:28-29)
until_text: Egeria (c. 384) found 'the city of Heroes' reduced to a village; a Roman fort stood there (Ero castra). No later evidence of Greek speakers.

bilingual_evidence: metropolis of the Heroopolite nome under the Ptolemies; Ptolemaic and Roman town at the canal to the Red Sea (Holladay's excavations)
status_evidence: metropolis of the Heroopolite nome (Strabo 17.1.26; Ptolemy); LXX Gen. 46:28
note: Identification of Heroonpolis with Tell el-Maskhuta is usual (Holladay); the Greek civic evidence is thin.

greek_from_text: metropolis of the Leontopolite nome under Rome (Strabo 17.1.19; Ptolemy); gymnasial order of the metropoleis from AD 4/5; boule from 200/201
until_text: Administration Roman to 641, then Arab. Speech: no Greek evidence after the 7th c.; the site was deserted in the Middle Ages. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).

bilingual_evidence: metropolis of the Leontopolite nome and, in the 5th-6th c., of Augustamnica II; Roman nome coins; Greek-writing bishops (431, 553); the Egyptian name lived on among Coptic speakers
status_evidence: metropolis of the Leontopolite nome; nome coins under Hadrian; provincial capital of Augustamnica II (Hierocles 728); metropolitan see (Metrodorus at Ephesus 431; Theodotus at Constantinople 553)
note: Not the Jewish Leontopolis of Onias (Tell el-Yahudiya).
sources: Strabo 17.1.19; Hierocles 728; Wikipedia: Leontopolis

period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
site: Tell el-Rub'a, near El-Simbillawein, Dakahlia Governorate
greek_from_text: Greek administration of the Mendesian nome under Ptolemy II (the hieroglyphic Mendes stele, c. 264 BC, records his works there)
until_text: The Mendesian branch silted and the town shrank in the late Ptolemaic and early Roman period; neighbouring Thmuis, 4 km south, became the metropolis, and the Greek-speaking class moved there.
fade_evidence: The town declined under the later Ptolemies and disappears from view in the 1st c. AD; Ptolemy and Aelius Aristides name Thmuis as the only town of note in the Mendesian nome.
ended_by: No named act: decline with the silting of the Mendesian branch; the nome capital moved to Thmuis.
bilingual_evidence: metropolis of the Mendesian nome under the Ptolemies; Ptolemaic Greek administration of the nome; Greek finds of the Ptolemaic town
status_evidence: metropolis of the Mendesian nome (Hdt. 2.42, 2.46; Strabo 17.1.19); capital of the 29th dynasty
note: The Greek-speaking community of Mendes itself is poorly documented; entered as a nome capital of the Ptolemaic period.
sources: Hdt. 2.46; Strabo 17.1.19; Redford, City of the Ram-Man (2010); Wikipedia: Mendes

site: El-Felusiyat, on the Bardawil lagoon, North Sinai Governorate
greek_from_text: road town on the march of Titus from Egypt to Judaea, AD 70 (Josephus, BJ 4.661); Pliny (5.68) lists it
until_text: Late Roman town with churches (Oren's excavations); bishops Theoctistus, Serapion and Abraham in the 4th-5th c.; the town declined after the Arab conquest of 639/640 and was later deserted at an unknown date. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850). Here the townspeople went over to Arabic.
fade_evidence: Three bishops of the 4th-5th c. (Le Quien); late Roman basilicas at El-Felusiyat. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
ended_by: No named act ended Greek speech. The coast road fell to the Arabs when 'Amr ibn al-'As marched from Palestine on Pelusium, winter 639/640 (Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam); the towns of the coast declined thereafter. Under Arab rule the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers kept in Arabic from 705/706 (al-Kindi); this ended Greek as the language of government, and no ban on Greek speech is recorded.
status_evidence: Hierocles 727; Georgius Cyprius; see suffragan of Pelusium
note: As with the other coast towns, the Greek-speaking population is inferred from the Greek name, its clergy and its finds.
sources: Josephus, BJ 4.661; Pliny, NH 5.68; Hierocles 727; Wikipedia: Ostracine

site: near El-Manzala, at the southern edge of Lake Manzala, Dakahlia Governorate (exact site uncertain)
greek_from_text: first attested as a see: bishop Philip at Nicaea, 325
until_text: John Cassian (c. 395) describes the district ruined by an incursion of the sea; bishops are attested into the 5th c. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Philip (325); Archebius (c. 395); no later Greek evidence. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
ended_by: No named act; the lagoon district passed to the Arabs in 641/642. Under Arab rule the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers kept in Arabic from 705/706 (al-Kindi); this ended Greek as the language of government, and no ban on Greek speech is recorded.
bilingual_evidence: see with bishop Philip at Nicaea 325; bishop Archebius (Cassian, Conl. 11.2); Hierocles
status_evidence: see (Philip at Nicaea 325; Archebius c. 395); Hierocles 727; Georgius Cyprius
note: Location near Lake Manzala is approximate; the Greek evidence is that of its clergy (Cassian met bishop Archebius, a former anchorite of the town).
sources: Cassian, Conlationes 7.26, 11.1-3; Hierocles 727; Timm, Das christlich-koptische Agypten

period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
other_names: Peremoun (Coptic); al-Farama (Arabic); Sin (Hebrew, Ezek. 30:15-16, if the same place)
site: Tell el-Farama, near Baluza, North Sinai Governorate
greek_from_text: Greek and Macedonian settlers, garrison and officials under the first Ptolemies (3rd c. BC); Greek mercenaries had held the place for Nectanebo II in 343 BC (Diod. 16.46-49) and Alexander entered it in 332 BC
until_text: Administration: Persian under Shahrbaraz 618/619-629, Arab from the winter of 639/640. Speech: the Greek-speaking elite of a metropolis survived into the 7th c.; after 640 the town (al-Farama) was a smaller Christian and Muslim garrison and market town; Greek probably faded in the 8th c. as Coptic and then Arabic took over. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Isidore of Pelusium's Greek letters (to c. 435); bishops at the councils to 451 and later; Greek remained in use under the Persians and early Arabs; no Greek documents of residents known after the 7th c. Papyri rarely survive in the wet Delta, so private Greek documents of residents are few. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
ended_by: Taken by the Persians under Shahrbaraz, 618/619; taken by 'Amr ibn al-'As after a siege of one to two months, winter 639/640 (Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam, Futuh Misr); no named act ended Greek speech. The later town was burnt by Baldwin I of Jerusalem in 1118. Under Arab rule the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers kept in Arabic from 705/706 (al-Kindi); this ended Greek as the language of government, and no ban on Greek speech is recorded.
pre_greek_note: The Hebrew Sin of Ezekiel is usually taken as Pelusium; the Egyptian name is not securely known (Coptic Peremoun may reflect an Egyptian Per-Amun).
bilingual_evidence: Ptolemaic and Roman port, customs station and garrison town with Greek settlers; metropolis of Augustamnica I; the some 2,000 Greek letters of Isidore of Pelusium (c. 400-435) address residents, clergy, teachers and officials of the town
status_evidence: royal port and fortress; Hellenistic and Roman town with theatre and baths (excavated); metropolis of Augustamnica I; bishop Dorotheus at Nicaea 325; Hierocles 726
note: Called bilingual: Greek was probably dominant in the late antique city (Isidore's letters), but an Egyptian-speaking population is presumed in a Delta port; Pelusium issued no civic coins and was not a polis in the Ptolemaic period. Tell el-Farama now lies in the North Sinai Governorate.
sources: Diod. 16.46-49; Strabo 17.1.21; Isidore of Pelusium, Letters; Carrez-Maratray, Peluse et l'angle oriental du delta (1999); Wikipedia: Pelusium

site: Faqus, Sharqia Governorate
greek_from_text: metropolis of the Arabian nome in Ptolemy (c. 150); Strabo (17.1.26) still calls it a village
until_text: Administration Roman to 640/641, then Arab. Speech: no Greek evidence after the 7th c. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Papyri rarely survive in the wet Delta, so private Greek documents of residents are few. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
ended_by: No named act: the district fell to 'Amr ibn al-'As in 640/641, after Pelusium and Bilbeis. Under Arab rule the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers kept in Arabic from 705/706 (al-Kindi); this ended Greek as the language of government, and no ban on Greek speech is recorded.
pre_greek_note: Faqus continues the ancient name; an Egyptian form is not securely attested.
bilingual_evidence: metropolis of the Arabian nome (Ptolemy); the see 'Arabia' of Augustamnica II
status_evidence: metropolis of the Arabian nome (Ptol. Geog. 4.5.53); see 'Arabia' (Hierocles 728)
note: Phakoussa has also been placed at Tell Faqus or near Qantir; the late antique see is called 'Arabia'.
sources: Strabo 17.1.26; Ptol. Geog. 4.5.53; Hierocles 728; Wikipedia: Faqous

site: Tell Mahrad, Wadi Feiran oasis, South Sinai Governorate
greek_from_text: first attested as a see: bishop Netras, a disciple of abba Silvanus, c. 400 (Apophthegmata Patrum)
until_text: Bishops to the 7th c. (Theodore of Pharan, Greek theologian, condemned in 680/681 as a Monothelete); after the Arab conquest of Sinai in the 630s-640s the town declined. The Greek-speaking monks of the fortified monastery of Sinai were a monastic community largely recruited from outside and do not extend the town's phase. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850). Here the townspeople went over to Arabic.
fade_evidence: Theodore of Pharan wrote Greek theology (c. 620-640); no Greek evidence for the town later. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
ended_by: No named act: Sinai passed to the Arabs in the 630s-640s; the town shrank in the following centuries. Under Arab rule the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers kept in Arabic from 705/706 (al-Kindi); this ended Greek as the language of government, and no ban on Greek speech is recorded.
pre_greek_note: Nabataean inscriptions of Sinai may name the oasis; not used here.
bilingual_evidence: see with Greek-writing bishops (Netras c. 400; Theodore, 7th c.); episcopal church with Greek inscriptions (Grossmann's excavations); local Saracen (Arab) population
status_evidence: see of Palaestina Tertia (bishops from c. 400 to the 7th c.); Pharan in Ptolemy, Geog. 5.17
note: A desert see with a mostly Arab population; the Greek-speaking community may have been only clergy and monks, which would rule it out.
sources: Apophthegmata Patrum (Netras); Ps.-Nilus, Narrationes; Grossmann, excavations at Pharan; Wikipedia: Pharan

site: Horbeit, near Abu Kebir, Sharqia Governorate
greek_from_text: metropolis of the Pharbaithite nome under Rome (Ptolemy 4.5); gymnasial order of the metropoleis from AD 4/5; boule from 200/201
until_text: Administration Roman to 641, then Arab. Speech: no Greek evidence after the 7th c. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Bishop Arbethion (325) and later bishops. Papyri rarely survive in the wet Delta, so private Greek documents of residents are few. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
ended_by: No named act: the treaty of Alexandria between the patriarch Cyrus and 'Amr ibn al-'As (November 641) handed Egypt to the Arabs; the Roman troops and many Greek-speaking officials and landowners left by September 642. Under Arab rule the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers kept in Arabic from 705/706 (al-Kindi); this ended Greek as the language of government, and no ban on Greek speech is recorded.
pre_greek_note: Horbeit is usually identified with Shedenu, capital of the 11th Lower Egyptian nome; the Greek name itself may come from an Egyptian Per-Horbeit.
bilingual_evidence: metropolis of the Pharbaithite nome; nome coins; bishop Arbethion at Nicaea 325
status_evidence: metropolis of the Pharbaithite nome; see (Nicaea 325); Hierocles 728
sources: Ptol. Geog. 4.5; Hierocles 728; Wikipedia: Horbeit

period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
site: El-Arish, North Sinai Governorate
greek_from_text: Hellenistic town on new ground (no earlier occupation found at El-Arish); a city on the border of Egypt and Syria in Strabo (16.2.31) and Diodorus (1.60)
until_text: Bishops from the 4th c. (Melas under Valens, Sozomen 6.31; Hermogenes at Ephesus 431); the town fell to the Arabs on 'Amr's march into Egypt, 639/640, and survived as al-Arish. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850). Here the townspeople went over to Arabic.
fade_evidence: Bishop Hermogenes (431), sent by Cyril of Alexandria to Rome; no Greek evidence after the 7th c. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
ended_by: No named act ended Greek speech. The coast road fell to the Arabs when 'Amr ibn al-'As marched from Palestine on Pelusium, winter 639/640 (Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam); the towns of the coast declined thereafter. Under Arab rule the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers kept in Arabic from 705/706 (al-Kindi); this ended Greek as the language of government, and no ban on Greek speech is recorded.
pre_greek_note: The legend of nose-cut exiles (Diodorus 1.60; Strabo 16.2.31) is not evidence of an earlier town.
status_evidence: city in Strabo and Diodorus; Hierocles 727; see (Melas, Solon; Hermogenes at Ephesus 431)
note: Population probably mixed (Greek, Egyptian, Idumaean and Arab); Greek counted as the main civic language for lack of evidence of another.
sources: Strabo 16.2.31; Diod. 1.60; Sozomen, HE 6.31; Hierocles 727; Wikipedia: Rhinocorura

period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
site: Samannud, Gharbia Governorate
greek_from_text: Manetho, priest of Sebennytos, wrote his history of Egypt in Greek for Ptolemy II, c. 280 BC
until_text: Administration Roman to 641, then Arab. Speech: the Greek-speaking metropolitan class is not attested after the 7th c.; the town became Coptic- and then Arabic-speaking. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Bishops of Sebennytos in late antiquity and later Coptic bishops. Papyri rarely survive in the wet Delta, so private Greek documents of residents are few. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
ended_by: No named act: the treaty of Alexandria between the patriarch Cyrus and 'Amr ibn al-'As (November 641) handed Egypt to the Arabs; the Roman troops and many Greek-speaking officials and landowners left by September 642. Under Arab rule the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers kept in Arabic from 705/706 (al-Kindi); this ended Greek as the language of government, and no ban on Greek speech is recorded.
bilingual_evidence: Manetho of Sebennytos wrote his Aegyptiaca in Greek (c. 280 BC); metropolis of the Sebennyte nome with the Roman metropolitan order; see
status_evidence: metropolis of the Sebennyte nome (Strabo 17.1.19; nome coins); see; Hierocles
note: Manetho shows a Greek-educated priest rather than a Greek community; the Greek civic class is presumed from the metropolis status.
sources: Manetho, Aegyptiaca (FGrHist 609); Strabo 17.1.19; Timm, Das christlich-koptische Agypten; Wikipedia: Sebennytos

site: Tell Hebua (with Tell Abu Sefa), about 4 km north-east of El-Qantara East, Ismailia Governorate
greek_from_text: first attested as a see: bishop Alypius at the Council of Ephesus, 431
until_text: Known only from one bishop, in 431; no later evidence. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Bishop Alypius (431); nothing later. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
ended_by: No named act; the eastern frontier fell to 'Amr ibn al-'As at the start of the conquest (Pelusium, 639-640). Under Arab rule the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers kept in Arabic from 705/706 (al-Kindi); this ended Greek as the language of government, and no ban on Greek speech is recorded.
pre_greek_note: the frontier fortress of Tjaru of the New Kingdom (Tell Hebua)
bilingual_evidence: see with bishop Alypius at the Council of Ephesus, 431 (Worp 1994); a fort and road station on the road from Pelusium into Egypt (Itinerarium Antonini; Notitia Dignitatum, an ala at Sele)
status_evidence: see (Alypius at Ephesus 431; Worp 1994); suffragan of Pelusium in Augustamnica I; Roman fort (Notitia Dignitatum)
note: A frontier fortress and road station whose see is known from one bishop. The garrison does not count; a Greek-speaking civilian community is only inferred from the see, as for the other see-only towns. Doubtful case.
sources: Worp, ZPE 100 (1994), checklist of bishops of Egypt AD 325 - c. 750; Acts of the Council of Ephesus (431), lists of bishops; Itinerarium Antonini; Notitia Dignitatum, Or. 28

site: Damietta (the old town lay nearer the sea; it was razed and rebuilt inland in 1250), Damietta Governorate
greek_from_text: first attested as a see: bishop at the council of Ephesus, 431
until_text: Administration Roman to 641/642, then Arab; the population was Coptic-speaking Christian and then Arabic. Greek raids on Damietta (853 and later) did not restore Greek speech. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Four bishops known from 431 to 879 (Le Quien). Papyri rarely survive in the wet Delta, so private Greek documents of residents are few. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
ended_by: No named act ended Greek; the town was taken by an Arab detachment sent by 'Amr ibn al-'As, 641/642 (later Arabic tradition). Under Arab rule the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers kept in Arabic from 705/706 (al-Kindi); this ended Greek as the language of government, and no ban on Greek speech is recorded.
pre_greek_note: Coptic Tamiati; an earlier Egyptian form is not securely attested.
bilingual_evidence: see with bishops from 431; city in Stephanus of Byzantium
status_evidence: see (bishop at Ephesus 431); Stephanus of Byzantium s.v.
note: A small town in late antiquity; it became important only in the Arab period.
sources: Steph. Byz. s.v. Ταμίαθις; Le Quien, Oriens Christianus II; Catholic Encyclopedia: Damietta

period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
site: San el-Hagar, Sharqia Governorate
greek_from_text: Ptolemaic Greek inscriptions and Greek administration of the Tanite nome, 3rd c. BC
until_text: Administration: Roman to 641, then Arab. Speech: the Greek-speaking metropolitan class is the last attested in the 6th-7th c.; Tanis shrank in the Arab period, but Coptic bishops of Tanis are known into the Middle Ages, so the population turned Coptic and then Arabic. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Bishops of Tanis at the councils (325 onwards); later Coptic bishops. Papyri rarely survive in the wet Delta, so private Greek documents of residents are few. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
ended_by: No named act: the treaty of Alexandria between the patriarch Cyrus and 'Amr ibn al-'As (November 641) handed Egypt to the Arabs; the Roman troops and many Greek-speaking officials and landowners left by September 642. Under Arab rule the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers kept in Arabic from 705/706 (al-Kindi); this ended Greek as the language of government, and no ban on Greek speech is recorded.
bilingual_evidence: metropolis of the Tanite nome; Ptolemaic Greek inscriptions (the bilingual Canopus decree of 238 BC was found here, 1866); Ptolemaic and Roman town (Petrie's excavations); bishop Tiberius at Nicaea 325
status_evidence: metropolis of the Tanite nome; nome coins under Trajan and Hadrian; see (bishop Tiberius at Nicaea 325); Hierocles 726
note: Capital of the 21st and 22nd dynasties; the Greek-period town occupied part of the old tell.
sources: Strabo 17.1.20; Petrie, Tanis I-II (1885-1888); Timm, Das christlich-koptische Agypten; Wikipedia: Tanis

site: Tell Tinnis, island in Lake Manzala, south-west of Port Said, Port Said Governorate
greek_from_text: island town and see visited by John Cassian (c. 395), who found its bishop just dead
until_text: Administration: Roman to 641/642, then Arab. Speech: the town grew under the Arabs into a great linen centre with a mostly Christian (Coptic-speaking) population; no Greek-speaking community is attested after the 7th c. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Bishop Heron (451); the monk Bernard found the people nearly all Christians c. 870. Papyri rarely survive in the wet Delta, so private Greek documents of residents are few. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
ended_by: No named act ended Greek; the treaty of Alexandria between the patriarch Cyrus and 'Amr ibn al-'As (November 641) handed Egypt to the Arabs; the Roman troops and many Greek-speaking officials and landowners left by September 642. Much later Saladin had the civilian town evacuated (1192/93), and the remaining fort was razed after the Fifth Crusade (1220s). Under Arab rule the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers kept in Arabic from 705/706 (al-Kindi); this ended Greek as the language of government, and no ban on Greek speech is recorded.
bilingual_evidence: see with bishops (Heron, condemned at Chalcedon 451); city in Hierocles; Roman-period tombs on the island
status_evidence: Hierocles 727; see suffragan of Pelusium (bishop at Chalcedon 451)
sources: Cassian, Conlationes 11.1-3; Hierocles 727; Encyclopaedia of Islam: Tinnis; Wikipedia: Thennesus

period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
site: Tell Timai, near Tmai el-Amdid, Dakahlia Governorate
greek_from_text: Greek mosaic signed by Sophilos with the portrait of Berenike II, c. 200 BC (Alexandria, Graeco-Roman Museum)
until_text: Administration: Roman to 641, then Arab. Speech: a Greek-educated civic class to late antiquity (Phileas, a rich man who had held civic offices, wrote in Greek; Serapion wrote Greek theology); later the bishops of Thmuis appear in Coptic sources. Greek probably faded in the 8th c. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Phileas' Greek letter (Eus. HE 8.10); Serapion's Greek works and the Euchologion; late Roman finds on site. Papyri rarely survive in the wet Delta, so private Greek documents of residents are few. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
ended_by: No named act: the treaty of Alexandria between the patriarch Cyrus and 'Amr ibn al-'As (November 641) handed Egypt to the Arabs; the Roman troops and many Greek-speaking officials and landowners left by September 642. Phileas of Thmuis was executed in the persecution of Diocletian, c. 306 (Eus. HE 8.9-10). Under Arab rule the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers kept in Arabic from 705/706 (al-Kindi); this ended Greek as the language of government, and no ban on Greek speech is recorded.
pre_greek_note: Coptic Thmoui; an Egyptian form is not securely attested.
bilingual_evidence: Hellenistic mosaics signed in Greek by Sophilos (c. 200 BC); Greek tax rolls of the town (P. Thmouis 1, 2nd c. AD, found on site); the bishops and Greek writers Phileas (d. c. 306) and Serapion (c. 339-360)
status_evidence: metropolis of the Mendesian (later Thmuite) nome in Roman times; boule; see (Phileas d. c. 306; a bishop at Nicaea 325; Serapion c. 339-360; Ptolemaeus at Seleucia 359; Aristobulus at Ephesus 431); Hierocles 726
note: Grew beside Mendes and replaced it as the nome capital in the Roman period.
sources: Eus. HE 8.9-10; Kambitsis, Le papyrus Thmouis 1 (1985); Littman and Silverstein, Tell Timai project; Wikipedia: Thmuis

site: Sheikh Ibada, Mallawi district, Minya Governorate
greek_from_text: Founded by Hadrian in the autumn of 130 where Antinous drowned in the Nile (Cassius Dio 69.11; Antinoite papyri).
until_text: Administration: Greek stayed the language of the tax and land registers under the first Arab governors; Arabic replaced it in the registers in 705/706 by order of the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik (al-Kindi). Speech: Antinoe remained a see and a town until it was abandoned around the 10th c., but its late texts are Coptic and Arabic; the Greek-speaking element faded in the 7th-8th c. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Seat of the governors of the Thebaid in the 6th c. (Dioscorus of Aphrodito wrote Greek poems and documents here); buildings of the Colluthus shrine in use to about the Arab conquest; later Coptic and Arabic writing exercises and a Coptic funerary stele dated 871. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
ended_by: No named act ended Greek speech. Occupied by the Persians (619-629); the Thebaid passed to the Arabs under the treaty of Alexandria concluded with 'Amr ibn al-'As (641); the registers were put into Arabic in 705/706 under the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik (al-Kindi).
pre_greek_note: A temple of Ramesses II and an earlier settlement lay at the site; it is often identified with the Hermopolite town Hir-wer, which is not certain.
bilingual_evidence: Founded with Greek settlers (many from Ptolemais Hermiou) under laws modelled on Naukratis, with tribes and demes, a boule and the Antinoeia games; from the 5th-6th c. a large Coptic-speaking Christian population (cult of St Colluthus, Coptic petitions and texts) beside the Greek civic and governing elite of the capital of the Thebaid
status_evidence: Greek polis founded by Hadrian (130) with boule, prytanis and Antinoite citizenship; home of the 4th-c. mathematician Serenus; see with bishops from 325 (Tyrannos, Loukios), later metropolitan see; capital of the Thebaid from the 4th c.; Hierocles (Thebaid)
sources: Cassius Dio 69.11; Zahrnt, ANRW II.10.1 (1988); Worp, ZPE 100 (1994); Wikipedia: Antinoopolis

period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
site: Atfih, Giza Governorate
greek_from_text: Greek settlers and Greek documents of the Aphroditopolite nome from the mid-3rd c. BC (Ptolemaic papyri, including the Zenon archive).
until_text: Administration: Greek stayed the language of the tax and land registers under the first Arab governors; Arabic replaced it in the registers in 705/706 by order of the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik (al-Kindi). Speech: the town shifted to Coptic and then Arabic in the 7th-8th c.; no local evidence dates the end more closely. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Listed with Nilopolis in a 7th-c. Greek levy account of the cities of Arcadia (SB I 5337); few later Greek documents from the town; Coptic see of Petpeh continued after the conquest. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
ended_by: No named act ended Greek speech. The town was occupied by the Persians (619-629) and taken by the army of 'Amr ibn al-'As in 640/641; the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers put into Arabic in 705/706 (al-Kindi). After that Greek faded as residents went over to Coptic and then Arabic.
pre_greek_note: Temple of Hathor and a cow necropolis at the site.
bilingual_evidence: metropolis of the Aphroditopolite nome; Greek papyri naming its residents from the Ptolemaic period on; city of Arcadia in Hierocles; see
status_evidence: metropolis of the Aphroditopolite nome; Hierocles (Arcadia); see with bishops Theodoros (before 339), Serenos (339), Chrysaorios (431)
note: Greek civic life here is known mostly from its status as a nome metropolis; local Greek texts are few.
sources: Hierocles, Synecdemus (Arcadia); Bowman & Rathbone, JRS 82 (1992); Gonis, Tyche 37 (2022); Trismegistos Geo 236; Worp, ZPE 100 (1994)

period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
other_names: Krokodilon polis, 'Krokodilopolis' (Greek, earlier name); Ptolemais Euergetis (Greek, Ptolemaic and Roman official name); Shedet (Egyptian); Piom (Coptic, also the name of the Fayum)
site: Kiman Faris (Kom Faris), Medinet el-Fayum, Faiyum Governorate
greek_from_text: Greek cleruchs settled in the newly drained Fayum under Ptolemy II from the 260s BC; the nome was named Arsinoite after Arsinoe II by c. 257 BC and Krokodilopolis was its metropolis.
until_text: Administration: Greek stayed the language of the tax and land registers under the first Arab governors; Arabic replaced it in the registers in 705/706 by order of the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik (al-Kindi). Speech: Greek survived in the Fayum mainly as a language of accounts into the second half of the 8th c.; Coptic took over private and legal documents in the 7th-8th c. and Arabic followed. Greek as a spoken language of residents probably ended before the last Greek accounts.
fade_evidence: Pahlavi papyri from the Fayum under the Persian occupation (619-629); Greek and Greek-Arabic documents of the Arsinoite pagarchy under the Umayyads; Greek accounting documents from the Fayum (Vienna fragments, Naqlun) into the second half of the 8th c.; Coptic dominant thereafter.
ended_by: No named act ended Greek speech. The Fayum was occupied by the Persians (619-629) and fell to the army of 'Amr ibn al-'As in 640/641 after the Roman commander John was killed (John of Nikiu, ch. 111-112); the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers put into Arabic in 705/706 (al-Kindi).
pre_greek_note: Modern 'Fayum' continues Coptic Piom, from Egyptian pa-yom 'the lake', a name of the region and later of the city.
bilingual_evidence: gymnasium and gymnasial class from the Ptolemaic period; the privileged '6,475 Greek men' (katoikoi) of the nome in the Roman period; boule from 200/201; thousands of Greek letters, contracts and literary papyri of residents; Demotic temple and private documents beside them
status_evidence: metropolis of the Arsinoite nome; gymnasium (Ptolemaic papyri); boule from 200/201; Christian teachers here debated with Dionysius of Alexandria c. 255 (Eus. HE 7.24); see with bishops from 325 (Melas) to Abraamios (c. 740); Hierocles (Arcadia)
note: Kept as a bilingual city: the Greek settler element was unusually large, but Egyptian priests, Demotic contracts and later Coptic show that Greek was not the language of the whole town.
sources: Bowman & Rathbone, JRS 82 (1992); Mueller, Settlement of the Ptolemies (2006); Bagnall, Egypt in Late Antiquity (1993); Worp, ZPE 100 (1994)

other_names: Babylon (Coptic); Babalyun, Qasr al-Sham' (Arabic); Kheriaha (Egyptian, earlier settlement nearby)
site: Qasr al-Sham', Old Cairo, Cairo Governorate
greek_from_text: Fortress by the Nile canal from Trajan's time (Amnis Traianus), rebuilt under Diocletian c. 300; first attested as a see with bishop Kyros at the council of Ephesus in 449.
until_text: Administration: Greek stayed the language of the tax and land registers under the first Arab governors; Arabic replaced it in the registers in 705/706 by order of the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik (al-Kindi). Speech: the Greek-speaking part of the population (officials, Chalcedonian clergy, merchants) shrank after 641 and was absorbed into the Coptic- and then Arabic-speaking population of Fustat.
fade_evidence: Greek remained the chancery language of the Arab governors at Fustat beside Babylon until 705/706; Greek-Arabic protocols and bilingual documents of the Umayyad period; Coptic and then Arabic took over in the churches of the fortress.
ended_by: The fortress surrendered to 'Amr ibn al-'As after a siege of about seven months (December 640 or April 641; John of Nikiu); the Arab camp-city Fustat was founded beside it (641/642); the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers put into Arabic in 705/706 (al-Kindi). No act against Greek speech is recorded.
pre_greek_note: The Egyptian settlement Kheriaha lay nearby; its exact relation to the Roman fortress town is not certain.
bilingual_evidence: a large late Roman fortress town with churches, clergy and officials; see from the 5th c.; Greek-speaking officials and soldiers are well attested, a Greek-speaking civic body of residents much less clearly
status_evidence: Roman fortress (Strabo 17.1.30; Notitia Dignitatum); see with bishops Kyros (449), Photios (459), Zosimos (c. 560), Theodoros (c. 743), Konstantinos (c. 755)
note: City status rests on the see and the size of the town; Greek speakers attested here are mostly officials and soldiers. Later see lists put it under Leontopolis (Augustamnica II) rather than Arcadia; Delta listings may also claim it.
sources: Strabo 17.1.30; John of Nikiu, Chronicle 111-117; Sheehan, Babylon of Egypt (2010); Worp, ZPE 100 (1994)

period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
other_names: Qs (Egyptian, per Trismegistos; older works give Saka or Hardai); Kais / Koeis (Coptic); el-Qays (Arabic)
site: El-Qays, Beni Mazar district, Minya Governorate
greek_from_text: Greek settlers and documents of the Kynopolite nome from the Ptolemaic period; firm civic evidence only in the Roman period.
until_text: Administration: Greek stayed the language of the tax and land registers under the first Arab governors; Arabic replaced it in the registers in 705/706 by order of the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik (al-Kindi). Speech: with few documents from the town itself, the end is placed with the general shift of Middle Egypt to Coptic and Arabic. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Few late Greek documents from the town; Coptic Kais survives as Arabic el-Qays. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
ended_by: No named act ended Greek speech. The town was occupied by the Persians (619-629) and taken by the army of 'Amr ibn al-'As in 640/641; the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers put into Arabic in 705/706 (al-Kindi). After that Greek faded as residents went over to Coptic and then Arabic.
pre_greek_note: Trismegistos gives Egyptian Qs, the source of Coptic Kais and Arabic el-Qays; older works call the capital of the 17th Upper Egyptian nome Saka or Hardai, and which lay under the Roman metropolis is debated.
bilingual_evidence: metropolis of the Kynopolite nome; Greek papyri of the nome; city of Arcadia in Hierocles; see
status_evidence: metropolis of the Kynopolite nome; Hierocles (Arcadia); see with bishops from 325 (Aiglon, Adamantios) to Gregorios (c. 680)
note: The Roman metropolis is usually put at el-Qays on the west bank; the dog necropolis is on the east bank near Hamatha. Distinct from Kynopolis in the Delta.
sources: Ptolemy, Geography 4.5; Hierocles, Synecdemus (Arcadia); Trismegistos Geo 1196; Worp, ZPE 100 (1994)

period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
site: Ihnasya el-Medina (Kom el-Aqarib), Beni Suef Governorate
greek_from_text: Greek settlers and Greek documents of residents of the Herakleopolite from the mid-3rd c. BC (Hibeh papyri).
until_text: Administration: Greek stayed the language of the tax and land registers under the first Arab governors; Arabic replaced it in the registers in 705/706 by order of the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik (al-Kindi). Speech: Greek documents of the Herakleopolite pagarchy continue into the 8th c., mostly as administration and accounts; the residents of the town (Ahnas) went over to Coptic and then Arabic.
fade_evidence: One of the earliest dated Arabic papyri is a Greek-Arabic receipt of 25 April 643 from Herakleopolis for sheep handed by the agents of the pagarchs Theodorakios and Christophoros to 'Abd Allah ibn Jabir and his troops (PERF 558); bilingual Greek-Arabic documents of the pagarchy in the Umayyad period; an 8th-c. Greek account found at Naqlun probably comes from the Herakleopolite; Coptic dominant afterwards.
ended_by: No named act ended Greek speech. The town was occupied by the Persians (619-629) and taken by the army of 'Amr ibn al-'As in 640/641; the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers put into Arabic in 705/706 (al-Kindi). After that Greek faded as residents went over to Coptic and then Arabic.
bilingual_evidence: Greek cleruchs in the nome from the 3rd c. BC; a Greek-speaking Jewish politeuma at Herakleopolis (papyri of 144-132 BC); gymnasial class; boule from 200/201; Greek papyri of residents into the Arab period
status_evidence: metropolis of the Herakleopolite nome; gymnasial class; boule from 200/201; see with bishops from 325 (Petros); Hierocles (Arcadia)
sources: Bowman & Rathbone, JRS 82 (1992); Cowey & Maresch, Urkunden des Politeuma der Juden von Herakleopolis (2001); PERF 558; Worp, ZPE 100 (1994)

period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
site: El-Ashmunein, Mallawi district, Minya Governorate
greek_from_text: Greek cavalry settlers of the Hermopolite dedicated a sanctuary to Ptolemy III and Berenike II (246-221 BC) in the city.
until_text: Administration: Greek stayed the language of the tax and land registers under the first Arab governors; Arabic replaced it in the registers in 705/706 by order of the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik (al-Kindi). Speech: Greek and Greek-Arabic documents of the Hermopolite continue into the 8th c.; the medieval town el-Ashmunein was Coptic-speaking and later Arabic-speaking (its 10th-c. bishop Severus wrote in Arabic).
fade_evidence: Pahlavi papyri from Hermopolis under the Persian occupation (619-629); Greek and bilingual documents of the Hermopolite pagarchy under the Umayyads; Coptic dominant in private documents from the 7th-8th c.; Severus ibn al-Muqaffa', bishop of el-Ashmunein, writing in Arabic in the 10th c.
ended_by: No named act ended Greek speech. The town was occupied by the Persians (619-629) and passed to the Arabs with the rest of Upper Egypt under the treaty of Alexandria concluded with 'Amr ibn al-'As (641); the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers put into Arabic in 705/706 (al-Kindi). After that Greek faded as residents went over to Coptic and then Arabic.
bilingual_evidence: Ptolemaic sanctuary dedicated to Ptolemy III and Berenike II by the cavalry settlers of the nome; gymnasium and gymnasial class; boule from 200/201 with a large council archive; thousands of Greek papyri of residents into the Arab period
status_evidence: metropolis of the Hermopolite nome; gymnasium; boule from 200/201; see with bishops from 325 (Phasileus); Hierocles (Thebaid)
note: In the Heptanomia until Diocletian, then in the Thebaid (Lower Thebaid).
sources: Bowman & Rathbone, JRS 82 (1992); Drew-Bear, Le nome Hermopolite (1979); Worp, ZPE 100 (1994); Wace, Megaw & Skeat, Hermopolis Magna: The Ptolemaic Sanctuary and the Basilica (1959); Wikipedia: Hermopolis

site: Ausim, Giza Governorate
greek_from_text: nome metropolis under Rome: the Greek-speaking metropolite and gymnasial class was registered in every metropolis from AD 4/5 (boule from 200/201); no earlier town-specific Greek evidence found; metropolis of the Letopolite nome; Hierocles (Arcadia); see with bishops Isaak (325), Gamul (c. 728), Moses (c. 735)
until_text: Administration: Greek stayed the language of the tax and land registers under the first Arab governors; Arabic replaced it in the registers in 705/706 by order of the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik (al-Kindi).
