After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Letopolite nome still a fiscal district in a 7th-c. Greek levy account of Arcadia (SB I 5337); no dated late Greek texts of residents; Coptic see of Boushem continued after the conquest. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
ended_by: No named act ended Greek speech. The town was occupied by the Persians (619-629) and taken by the army of 'Amr ibn al-'As in 640/641; the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers put into Arabic in 705/706 (al-Kindi). After that Greek faded as residents went over to Coptic and then Arabic.
pre_greek_note: Coptic Boushem / Oushem and Arabic Ausim continue it.
bilingual_evidence: metropolis of the Letopolite nome in the Roman period (Ptolemy, Geography 4.5); still a fiscal district in a 7th-c. Greek account of Arcadia; city of Arcadia in Hierocles; see; few Greek documents of residents survive
status_evidence: metropolis of the Letopolite nome; Hierocles (Arcadia); see with bishops Isaak (325), Gamul (c. 728), Moses (c. 735)
note: Lies at the apex of the Delta and may also be claimed for Lower Egypt; Greek-speaking residents are inferred from its status as a metropolis more than shown by local texts.
sources: Hierocles, Synecdemus (Arcadia); Ptolemy, Geography 4.5; Gonis, Tyche 37 (2022); Worp, ZPE 100 (1994)

other_names: Men-nefer and Inbu-hedj, 'White Walls' (Egyptian); Menfe / Memfi (Coptic); Manf (medieval Arabic)
site: Mit Rahina, Badrashin district, Giza Governorate
greek_from_text: Ionian and Carian soldiers moved by Amasis (570-526 BC) from the Stratopeda to Memphis as his guard (Hdt. 2.154); their descendants are the Hellenomemphites of later documents. Bilingual civic body under the Ptolemies and Romans.
until_text: Administration: Greek stayed the language of the tax and land registers under the first Arab governors; Arabic replaced it in the registers in 705/706 by order of the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik (al-Kindi). Speech: Memphis lost its people to the new Arab capital Fustat beside Babylon (founded 641/642) and was quarried for its stone; the Greek-speaking element faded in the 7th-8th c. while the Christian population kept Coptic. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Greek inscriptions and papyri of Memphis run into the 6th-7th c.; the town was a see (the Melitian leader John Arkaph was its bishop, c. 330s) and remained a Coptic see after the conquest; Fustat drew away its population from 641/642; Arabic replaced Greek in the registers in 705/706. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
ended_by: No named act ended Greek speech. Memphis was occupied by the Persians (619-629) and fell to the army of 'Amr ibn al-'As with the surrender of Babylon (640/641); the founding of Fustat (641/642) and the later removal of its stone for Fustat and Cairo emptied the town; the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers put into Arabic in 705/706 (al-Kindi).
pre_greek_note: Also called Inbu-hedj, 'White Walls' (Egyptian).
bilingual_evidence: Greek quarter of the Hellenomemphites with its Hellenion from the 6th c. BC (Hdt. 2.154; Ptolemaic papyri); Greek letters of residents such as the Serapeum archive of Ptolemaios son of Glaukias (2nd c. BC, beside Demotic); nome metropolis with a gymnasial class and, from 200/201, a boule
status_evidence: metropolis of the Memphite nome; Hellenomemphites and Hellenion; boule from 200/201; see by the early 4th c. (Antiochos, 325; the Melitian John Arkaph, 325-335); bishop Ptolemaios c. 700; Hierocles (Arcadia)
note: Greeks were a minority quarter here from the 6th c. BC; the bilingual civic body is Ptolemaic and Roman. Phase start is the settlement under Amasis, not a civic foundation.
sources: Hdt. 2.154; Thompson, Memphis under the Ptolemies (2nd ed. 2012); Bowman & Rathbone, JRS 82 (1992); Worp, ZPE 100 (1994)

other_names: Tilothis and Neilos (Greek); Tiloj / Telaj (Coptic); Dalas (Arabic)
site: Dalas, Beni Suef Governorate
greek_from_text: First evidence of a civic community: Chaeremon, aged bishop of Nilopolis, fled in the Decian persecution c. 250 (Dionysius of Alexandria in Eus. HE 6.42.3).
until_text: Administration: Greek ended in the registers in 705/706 (al-Kindi). Speech: no local Greek evidence after the 6th-7th c.; the town shifted to Coptic and then Arabic. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Its district was separate in the 4th-5th c., merged with Herakleopolis by 538 and separate again for taxes by the late 6th c.; listed with Aphroditopolis in a 7th-c. Greek levy account of Arcadia (SB I 5337); seat of a pagarchy in the later 8th c.; Coptic Tiloj survives as Arabic Dalas. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
ended_by: No named act ended Greek speech. The town was occupied by the Persians (619-629) and taken by the army of 'Amr ibn al-'As in 640/641; the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers put into Arabic in 705/706 (al-Kindi). After that Greek faded as residents went over to Coptic and then Arabic.
pre_greek_note: Egyptian form given in modern reference works; Greek Tilothis, Coptic Tiloj and Arabic Dalas continue it.
bilingual_evidence: see with a bishop by c. 250 (Chaeremon, Eus. HE 6.42.3); city of Arcadia in Hierocles; chief place of a toparchy of the Herakleopolite
status_evidence: see by c. 250 (Chaeremon, Eus. HE 6.42.3), then Theon (325), Eusebios (431); Hierocles (Arcadia); Ptolemy 4.5 (on an island in the Nile)
note: Not a nome metropolis; its Greek-speaking community is shown mainly by its early see. Placed at Dalas by the Coptic name; Ptolemy puts it on a Nile island.
sources: Eusebius, HE 6.42.3; Worp, ZPE 100 (1994); Gonis, Tyche 37 (2022); Trismegistos Geo 2427; Wikipedia: Delas

period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
other_names: Per-Medjed (Egyptian); Pemdje (Coptic); Nea Ioustinou polis (Greek honorific name after an emperor Justin, 6th c.); el-Bahnasa (Arabic)
site: El-Bahnasa, Beni Mazar district, Minya Governorate
greek_from_text: Greek cleruchs and Greek documents of residents of the Oxyrhynchite nome from the mid-3rd c. BC (Hibeh papyri).
until_text: Administration: Greek stayed the language of the tax and land registers under the first Arab governors; Arabic replaced it in the registers in 705/706 by order of the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik (al-Kindi). Speech: the dated Greek papyri from the town thin out after the 640s; the medieval town of el-Bahnasa spoke Coptic and then Arabic. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Greek documents of the Apion estate and the city to the 610s-620s; papyri dated by the Persian occupation (619-629); a few Greek documents of the early Arab period; Coptic then Arabic afterwards. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
ended_by: No named act ended Greek speech. Occupied by the Persians (619-629); taken by the army of 'Amr ibn al-'As in 640/641; the registers were put into Arabic in 705/706 under the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik (al-Kindi). The Arabic epic of the conquest of el-Bahnasa is legendary.
bilingual_evidence: gymnasium and gymnasial class; boule from 200/201; theatre; thousands of Greek private letters, contracts and literary papyri of residents (Oxyrhynchus Papyri); later the metropolitan see of Arcadia
status_evidence: metropolis of the Oxyrhynchite nome; gymnasium; boule from 200/201; see with bishops from 325 (Pelagios); Hierocles (Arcadia)
note: The origin of the Arabic name el-Bahnasa is uncertain, so no continuity with the Egyptian or Coptic name is claimed.
sources: Bowman et al., Oxyrhynchus: A City and its Texts (2007); Bowman & Rathbone, JRS 82 (1992); Trismegistos Geo 1524; Worp, ZPE 100 (1994)

site: unlocated, Fayum, Faiyum Governorate
greek_from_text: Named after Theodosius I or II; first attested in a Greek papyrus of 447 as a city with its own nome in the Fayum.
until_text: Administration: the Theodosiopolite nome was dissolved by the mid or later 7th c. and survived only as a subregion of the Arsinoite into the 8th c. Speech: its people followed the Fayum's shift to Coptic and Arabic in the 7th-8th c. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Greek papyri name the city and its nome from 447 (also P.Oxy. LI 3636, 5th c.); the joint pagarchy of Arsinoe and Theodosiopolis last appears in 622 (CPR XIX 32) and the Theodosiopolite nome in 644 (BGU I 320); traces of it as a part of the Arsinoite in the 8th c. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
ended_by: No named act. The Fayum fell to the army of 'Amr ibn al-'As in 640/641 (John of Nikiu); the separate nome was merged back into the Arsinoite under Arab rule; the registers were put into Arabic in 705/706 under the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik.
bilingual_evidence: a city (civitas) with its own nome carved from the Arsinoite, attested in Greek papyri from 447; city of Arcadia in Hierocles; its affairs were run by officials of Arsinoe; no bishop of its own is recorded
status_evidence: Hierocles (Arcadia); Greek papyri from 447 (city and nome); no bishop recorded
note: Site unknown: Tebtunis has been proposed but is doubted. A 'formal city' administered from Arsinoe, so a Greek-speaking civic body of its own is not clearly shown.
sources: Hierocles, Synecdemus (Arcadia); Tyche: 'The City Solution? Theodosiopolis and the System of Joint Administration in the Late Antique Fayyum'; Gonis, Tyche 37 (2022); Trismegistos Geo 2375

other_names: Toou (Greek form of the earlier village name)
site: Taha el-Amida (Taha el-Amudein), Minya district, Minya Governorate
greek_from_text: Promoted to a city and named after Theodosius I or II, so by 450 at the latest; attested as a city by Hierocles (c. 527).
until_text: Administration: Greek ended in the registers in 705/706 (al-Kindi). Speech: no local Greek evidence after the 6th-7th c.; the area followed the Hermopolite shift to Coptic and then Arabic. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: No dated Greek texts of residents are known from the town itself; the Hermopolite as a whole has Greek documents into the 8th c. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
ended_by: No named act ended Greek speech. The town was occupied by the Persians (619-629) and passed to the Arabs with the rest of Upper Egypt under the treaty of Alexandria concluded with 'Amr ibn al-'As (641); the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers put into Arabic in 705/706 (al-Kindi). After that Greek faded as residents went over to Coptic and then Arabic.
pre_greek_note: The city was the former village Toou (Greek spelling); its Egyptian form is not given here because it is not securely attested.
bilingual_evidence: city of the Thebaid in Hierocles; created out of the Hermopolite nome, whose towns have abundant Greek documents
status_evidence: Hierocles (Thebaid); no bishop recorded
note: The Barrington Atlas (75 D4) identifies Theodosiopolis with the village Toou at Taha el-Amida north of Minya; whether the Arabic name continues Toou is not certain. Not to be confused with Theodosiopolis in the Fayum.
sources: Hierocles, Synecdemus (Thebaid); Barrington Atlas 75 D4; Trismegistos Geo 3383; Timm, Das christlich-koptische Ägypten

site: Qaw el-Kebir (El-Etmaniya), Asyut Governorate (El-Badari district)
greek_from_text: nome metropolis under Rome: the Greek-speaking metropolite and gymnasial class was registered in every metropolis from AD 4/5 (boule from 200/201); no earlier town-specific Greek evidence found; metropolis of the Antaiopolite nome; temple of Antaios built under Ptolemy IV, enlarged under Ptolemy VI and restored under Marcus Aurelius (Greek dedications); see; Hierocles (Ἀνταίου)
until_text: Speech: Greek-writing landowners and officials of the city are attested to the 7th c.; the population spoke Coptic. Administration: the pagarchy of Antaiopolis continued under Arab rule with Greek and Coptic paperwork until Arabic began replacing Greek in the government registers in 706 on the order of the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik (al-Kindi). After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Aphrodito papyri (6th c.) show Antaiopolite notables writing Greek; in the Thebaid Coptic replaced Greek as the language of private letters and contracts during the 6th and 7th c.; Greek survived longer in fiscal documents, protocols and among the landowning and clerical elite. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
ended_by: No named act ended Greek speech here: the Greek-speaking community faded by gradual shift to Coptic. Greek administration ended with the Arab conquest of Egypt by 'Amr ibn al-'As (Alexandria surrendered 641, evacuated 642; Upper Egypt passed under Arab rule with it); Arabic replaced Greek in the government registers in 706 on the order of the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik (al-Kindi).
bilingual_evidence: metropolis of the Antaiopolite nome; a see; seat of a boule and later a pagarchy; Greek contracts and petitions of its citizens in the 6th-c. Aphrodito papyri
status_evidence: metropolis of the Antaiopolite nome; temple of Antaios built under Ptolemy IV, enlarged under Ptolemy VI and restored under Marcus Aurelius (Greek dedications); see; Hierocles (Ἀνταίου)
note: The temple of Antaios, still standing in 1813, was swept away by the Nile in 1821.
sources: Bowman & Rathbone, JRS 82 (1992); MacCoull, Dioscorus of Aphrodito (1988); Wikipedia: Antaeopolis; Hierocles, Synecdemus

site: Kom Ishqaw, Sohag Governorate (Tahta district)
greek_from_text: nome metropolis under Rome: the Greek-speaking metropolite and gymnasial class was registered in every metropolis from AD 4/5 (boule from 200/201); no earlier town-specific Greek evidence found; metropolis of the Aphroditopolite nome (Ptolemy, Geog. 4.5; polis in documents of the 2nd c. BC - 2nd c. AD); a kome from the 3rd c. (Trismegistos Geo 237)
until_text: City status: metropolis in the early Roman period; a village (kome) of the Antaiopolite nome from the 3rd c. on, with autopragia granted under Leo I (457-474). Speech: Dioscorus' circle wrote Greek and Coptic (6th c.); the village archives of the early 8th c. are Coptic for residents' own affairs and Greek and Arabic for the governor's letters (Qurra ibn Sharik, 709-714). Administration: Arabic replaced Greek in the government registers in 706 on the order of the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik (al-Kindi).
fade_evidence: Dioscorus' Greek poems and contracts (c. 540-585); his own Coptic documents; Basileios archive 709-714: Greek letters of the governor, Coptic for village business; in the Thebaid Coptic replaced Greek as the language of private letters and contracts during the 6th and 7th c.; Greek survived longer in fiscal documents, protocols and among the landowning and clerical elite.
ended_by: No named act ended Greek speech here: the Greek-speaking community faded by gradual shift to Coptic. Greek administration ended with the Arab conquest of Egypt by 'Amr ibn al-'As (Alexandria surrendered 641, evacuated 642; Upper Egypt passed under Arab rule with it); Arabic replaced Greek in the government registers in 706 on the order of the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik (al-Kindi). The village came under the Arab pagarchy of Ishqaw in the early 8th c.
pre_greek_note: Per-Wadjet is given for Aphroditopolis of the 10th Upper Egyptian nome in standard lists; the identification with Kom Ishqaw is the usual one but not beyond doubt.
bilingual_evidence: metropolis of the Aphroditopolite nome in the early Roman period; later a large village whose landowners wrote Greek: Dioscorus of Aphrodito (c. 520-585), notary and Greek poet; Greek and Coptic archive of the pagarch Basileios (709-714)
status_evidence: metropolis of the Aphroditopolite nome (Ptolemy, Geog. 4.5; polis in documents of the 2nd c. BC - 2nd c. AD); a kome from the 3rd c. (Trismegistos Geo 237)
note: Counted for its metropolis phase; in the 6th c. (its best-documented period) it was legally a village, though larger than many cities.
sources: MacCoull, Dioscorus of Aphrodito (1988); Fournet (ed.), Les archives de Dioscore d'Aphrodité (2008); Wikipedia: Kom Ishqaw; Ptolemy, Geog. 4.5

site: Kom Isfaht, Asyut Governorate (Abu Tig district)
greek_from_text: metropolis of a separate nome by the early 2nd c. AD (archive of the strategos Apollonios, 113-120)
until_text: Speech: Greek-speaking metropolite class of the Roman period; shift to Coptic in the 6th-7th c. In the early Islamic period the district became the kura of Qahqawa. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Few documents from the town itself after the 2nd c.; in the Thebaid Coptic replaced Greek as the language of private letters and contracts during the 6th and 7th c.; Greek survived longer in fiscal documents, protocols and among the landowning and clerical elite. ended_by: No named act ended Greek speech here: the Greek-speaking community faded by gradual shift to Coptic. Greek administration ended with the Arab conquest of Egypt by 'Amr ibn al-'As (Alexandria surrendered 641, evacuated 642; Upper Egypt passed under Arab rule with it); Arabic replaced Greek in the government registers in 706 on the order of the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik (al-Kindi).
pre_greek_note: The Coptic name Sbeht (continued in Arabic Isfaht) is not Greek; its Egyptian original is not securely identified.
bilingual_evidence: metropolis of the Apollonopolite Heptakomias nome; Greek archive of the strategos Apollonios and his family (113-120); a city in Hierocles (Ἀπόλλωνος)
status_evidence: metropolis of the Apollonopolite Heptakomias nome (Apollonios archive, P.Giss., P.Brem.); Hierocles
note: Keep apart from Apollonopolis Mikra/Parva (Qus) and Apollonopolis Magna (Edfu). The Apollonios archive shows a strategos from Hermopolis, an official; the resident Greek-speaking class is inferred from metropolis status.
sources: Wikipedia: Kom Isfaht; Trismegistos Geo (Apollonopolis Heptakomias); Kortus, Briefe des Apollonios-Archives (1999); Bowman & Rathbone, JRS 82 (1992)

site: Edfu, Aswan Governorate

bilingual_evidence: metropolis of the Apollonopolite nome; Greek and Demotic ostraca of residents from the Ptolemaic period (Tell Edfu); a Jewish community with Greek names (Greek tax receipts, 1st c. AD); a see
status_evidence: metropolis of the Apollonopolite nome; see; Hierocles (Ἀπόλλωνος)
sources: Bagnall & Rathbone 2004; Fouilles franco-polonaises, Tell Edfou (1937-1950); Wikipedia: Edfu

site: Qus, Qena Governorate
greek_from_text: raised to a city as Diocletianopolis under the tetrarchs, c. 300 (first attestation as a city)
until_text: Speech: Greek-speaking civic and clerical class of the late Roman city; shift to Coptic in the 6th-7th c.; medieval Qus became the chief Muslim city of Upper Egypt. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).

bilingual_evidence: a city as Diocletianopolis in Hierocles and Georgius Cyprius (if the identification holds) and a see; Greek name of the town

Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.

Events: Diocletian withdrew the frontier from the Dodekaschoinos to Philae and Elephantine (298; Procopius, Wars 1.19); raids of the Blemmyes and Nobades in the 4th-5th c.; the Persian occupation of Egypt under Shahrbaraz (619-629); the Arab conquest of Egypt by 'Amr ibn al-'As (Alexandria surrendered 641, evacuated 642; Upper Egypt passed under Arab rule with it); Aswan was the base for 'Abd Allah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh's campaign against Makuria and the treaty (baqt) of 652; Arabic replaced Greek in the government registers in 706 on the order of the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik (al-Kindi).
other_language: Egyptian (Demotic, then Coptic); Nubian and Blemmyan neighbours
bilingual_evidence: Greek settlers at Syene and Elephantine from the early Ptolemaic period (P.Eleph. 1, 311 BC); Greek ostraca of residents (Ptolemaic and Roman); a see from the 4th c.; Greek family archive of Patermouthis, soldier and boatman of Syene and Elephantine (493-613)
status_evidence: see from the 4th c. (Bishop Appion of Syene, 425-450); Syene in Strabo and Ptolemy; Greek documents of residents
note: Syene was always a garrison town; it counts here for its Greek settler families, its see and the Patermouthis documents. The fort island of Elephantine opposite is treated with Syene.
sources: P.Eleph. 1; Farber & Porten, The Patermouthis Archive (in The Elephantine Papyri in English, 1996); Procopius, Wars 1.19; Wikipedia: Aswan

site: Dendera, Qena Governorate
greek_from_text: Greek dedication of the Isis propylon by 'those from the metropolis and the nome', year 31 of Augustus, AD 1/2 (OGIS 659; first attestation of the civic body); an earlier Greek dedication by the local strategos Ptolemaios son of Panas, 12 BC
until_text: Speech: Greek-speaking metropolite class of the Roman period; shift to Coptic in the 6th-7th c. Administration: the Arab conquest of Egypt by 'Amr ibn al-'As (Alexandria surrendered 641, evacuated 642; Upper Egypt passed under Arab rule with it); Arabic replaced Greek in the government registers in 706 on the order of the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik (al-Kindi). After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Pachomian sources (4th c.) show the bishop of Tentyra among Coptic-speaking monks; in the Thebaid Coptic replaced Greek as the language of private letters and contracts during the 6th and 7th c.; Greek survived longer in fiscal documents, protocols and among the landowning and clerical elite. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
ended_by: No named act ended Greek speech here: the Greek-speaking community faded by gradual shift to Coptic. Greek administration ended with the Arab conquest of Egypt by 'Amr ibn al-'As (Alexandria surrendered 641, evacuated 642; Upper Egypt passed under Arab rule with it); Arabic replaced Greek in the government registers in 706 on the order of the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik (al-Kindi).
bilingual_evidence: metropolis of the Tentyrite nome; Greek dedications of temple buildings by 'those from the metropolis and the nome' (propylon of the Isis temple, AD 1; pronaos of the Hathor temple, AD 35/36); see (Sarapion of Tentyra, 4th c.)
status_evidence: metropolis of the Tentyrite nome; Greek civic dedications (AD 1, AD 35/36); Juvenal 15 on the feud of Tentyra and Ombos (AD 127); see; Hierocles (Τέντυρα)
sources: OGIS 659; Juvenal 15; Vita prima Pachomii; Wikipedia: Dendera

period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
other_names: Diospolis Megale; Djeme (Coptic, the west-bank town); Luxor (Arabic al-Uqsur)
site: Luxor (Karnak and Luxor temples, east bank), Luxor Governorate
greek_from_text: Greek residents and Greek documents at Thebes from the 3rd c. BC
until_text: Speech: a Greek-speaking minority from the 3rd c. BC; Thebes was reduced to a group of villages after 88 BC (Strabo 17.1.46) but Greek ostraca of residents continue through the Roman period; in the 6th-8th c. the Theban towns (Djeme) used Coptic for their own contracts and letters, with Greek formulae and protocols. Administration: the Arab conquest of Egypt by 'Amr ibn al-'As (Alexandria surrendered 641, evacuated 642; Upper Egypt passed under Arab rule with it); Arabic replaced Greek in the government registers in 706 on the order of the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik (al-Kindi). After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Thousands of Greek ostraca from Thebes (Ptolemaic to 7th c.); the Coptic legal documents of Djeme (7th-8th c.); in the Thebaid Coptic replaced Greek as the language of private letters and contracts during the 6th and 7th c.; Greek survived longer in fiscal documents, protocols and among the landowning and clerical elite. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
ended_by: No named act ended Greek speech. Acts against the city: held by the rebel pharaohs Haronnophris and Chaonnophris in the great Theban revolt (206-186 BC); sacked by Ptolemy IX Soter II after the revolt of 88-86 BC (Pausanias 1.9.3); taken by C. Cornelius Gallus in the revolt of 29 BC (Philae stele); legionary fortress built in the Luxor temple under Diocletian (c. 300); the Arab conquest of Egypt by 'Amr ibn al-'As (Alexandria surrendered 641, evacuated 642; Upper Egypt passed under Arab rule with it); Arabic replaced Greek in the government registers in 706 on the order of the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik (al-Kindi).
bilingual_evidence: Greek residents from the 3rd c. BC (Greek tax receipts and bank documents; the lawsuit of the Greek officer Hermias over a house in Thebes, 117 BC); metropolis of the Theban nome with its gymnasial class in the Roman period
status_evidence: metropolis of the Theban nome (Diospolis Magna); Greek documents of residents
note: Arabic al-Uqsur ('the castles') refers to the Roman fortress and temples, not to an ancient name of the city. Strabo already describes Thebes as villages, but the Greek-writing community did not disappear.
sources: Pausanias 1.9.3; Strabo 17.1.46; Philae stele of Cornelius Gallus (29 BC); Wikipedia: Thebes, Egypt; Bagnall & Rathbone 2004

list_group: Red Sea coast and the oases
period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
other_names: Kleopatris (Strabo 17.1.25-26); Klysma (Roman and later; Hierocles); Peklousma (Coptic); al-Qulzum (Arabic, after the conquest; hence Bahr al-Qulzum, the Arabic name of the Red Sea)
site: Kom el-Qolzum (Tell el-Qulzum), north side of Suez, Suez Governorate
greek_from_text: founded by Ptolemy II at the head of the Gulf of Suez, at the end of his Nile-Red Sea canal, and named after his sister-wife Arsinoe II, c. 270 BC (Strabo 17.1.25-26; the Pithom stele records a foundation named Arsinoe, which may be this one); later renamed Kleopatris; rebuilt as Klysma under Trajan, early 2nd c. AD
until_text: Klysma was a Greek-speaking port town and bishop's see into the 6th c. (bishops to 553; pilgrims describe its port and church c. 570). Administration: taken with Egypt by the Arabs in 641; 'Amr ibn al-'As reopened the canal to the port, now al-Qulzum, to ship Egyptian grain to Arabia; Greek orders of the governor Qurra ibn Sharik (708-710) name it only as the base of the Arab fleet. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: bishops Iakob (before 347), Tithoes and Paulos (347), Poimen (458/459) and Stephanos (Council of Constantinople, 553) (Worp 1994); Egeria (c. 383/384) and the Piacenza pilgrim (c. 570) describe the port and its church; after the conquest Klysma appears in Greek papyri only as the base of the Arab fleet, in orders of the governor Qurra ibn Sharik to Aphrodito (P. Lond. IV 1346 and 1383, 708-710), which are administrative Greek, not evidence of Greek speakers at Klysma. Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
ended_by: Taken with the rest of Egypt by the Arabs under 'Amr ibn al-'As, 641; under the caliphs the port became al-Qulzum. No named act ended Greek speech there. Under Arab rule the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers kept in Arabic from 705/706 (al-Kindi); this ended Greek as the language of government, and no ban on Greek speech is recorded.
status_evidence: royal foundation of Ptolemy II (Pithom stele; Strabo 17.1.25-26); Klysma a bishop's see 347-553 (Worp, ZPE 100, 1994); Klysma listed by Hierocles (as a kastron)
note: The Ptolemaic town and Roman Klysma are usually placed at or near Kom el-Qolzum on the north side of Suez; some scholars put Arsinoe a few km away. Treated as one place; the mound is now largely built over.
sources: Strabo 17.1.25-26; Cohen 2006; Worp, ZPE 100 (1994); P. Lond. IV 1346; Trismegistos Geo 2794
refoundations: Arsinoe -> Kleopatris (renamed under a Cleopatra, same place) -> Klysma (rebuilt by Trajan, early 2nd c. AD; same area)

list_group: Red Sea coast and the oases
period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
other_names: Berenike Trogodytike; Berenike (Strabo, Pliny); the nearby modern town Berenice (Baranis) takes its name from it
site: Medinet el-Haras, south of the town of Berenice (Baranis), Red Sea Governorate
greek_from_text: founded by Ptolemy II and named after his mother Berenike I (Pliny NH 6.168; Strabo 17.1.45), c. 275 BC; the earliest excavated levels are of the 3rd c. BC
until_text: The port shrank in the late 3rd c., revived in the 4th-5th c. and was abandoned some time before the mid-6th c.; the last shrine went out of use by the early 6th c. The bay later silted up and the site was never reoccupied.
fade_evidence: Greek ostraca and papyri of the 1st c. AD (O. Berenike I-III) beside Latin, Tamil-Brahmi, Prakrit, Hebrew, Palmyrene and South Arabian texts; late Roman church; Greek inscriptions of Blemmyan kings (late 4th-5th c.); pottery of the last phase runs to the early 6th c.
ended_by: No named act: abandoned before the mid-6th c., after a last phase under Blemmyan kings (Isemne, Kabantia); the excavators point to the collapse of the Red Sea trade. No destruction is recorded.
other_language: Blemmyan (in the last phase, late 4th to early 6th c.), beside Egyptian
bilingual_evidence: in the last phase the town had a Blemmyan population and was apparently ruled by Blemmyan kings: Greek inscriptions of the late 4th-5th c. name the kings Isemne and Kabantia, and the late Falcon Shrine served Blemmyan worshippers (Oller Guzman et al., AJA 126, 2022); Greek remained the written language
status_evidence: royal foundation of Ptolemy II (Pliny NH 6.168); seat of the praefectus montis Berenicidis in the Roman period; Greek ostraca and papyri of residents; excavations 1994-2001 and from 2008
note: A multilingual port town (Greek, Egyptian, Latin, Indian, South Arabian and Aksumite visitors and residents); Greek was the main language of its documents. How far the Blemmyes controlled the last town is debated.
sources: Pliny NH 6.168; Strabo 17.1.45; Sidebotham, Berenike and the Ancient Maritime Spice Route (2011); Oller Guzman et al., AJA 126 (2022) 567-591; Cohen 2006

list_group: Red Sea coast and the oases
other_names: 'the city of Oasis' (Hdt. 3.26); Hibiton polis ('city of the Hibites'); Ibis; Hebet (Egyptian); metropolis of the Great Oasis (Oasis Magna); the town site is now called Ain Turba (Arabic)
site: Ain Turba and the Temple of Hibis, with the Bagawat necropolis to the north, 2-3 km north of El-Kharga, New Valley Governorate
greek_from_text: Greek-writing civic elite first clearly attested c. 300: the wealthy Hellenized households of Ain Turba (late 3rd-early 4th c., with an Iliad school tablet) and the councillors of the 4th c. Hibis had long been the seat of the administration of the Great Oasis (prefects' edicts of AD 49 and 68 published at its temple), but that is official Greek. Herodotus (3.26) says that in 525 BC 'the city of Oasis' was held by Samians 'said to be of the Aeschrionian tribe'; this single report is not counted as the start of a Greek city.
until_text: Administration: the oasis passed under Arab rule after the conquest of Egypt (641); Greek stayed in the government of Egypt until 706. Speech: Greek graffiti at Bagawat still name the 'polis of Hibis' in the 7th-8th c.; a Coptic graffito of 784-883 at Gebel el-Teir shows the town still existed, by then writing Coptic. Greek gave way to Coptic and then Arabic.
fade_evidence: 4th-c. Greek and Coptic ostraca and an Iliad school tablet from the Ain Turba houses (Bagnall & Tallet 2015); Greek graffiti at Bagawat of the 7th-8th c.; Coptic graffito of 784-883 at Gebel el-Teir
ended_by: No named act ended Greek: the Blemmyes raided the Oasis c. 440-450 and carried off the exiled Nestorius (Nestorius' letters in Evagrius, HE 1.7), and the nearby monastery of Deir el-Bagawat was given up in the mid-5th c., possibly after such raids, but the town survived; after the Arab conquest of Egypt by 'Amr ibn al-'As (641/642) Greek faded as Coptic and then Arabic took over.
bilingual_evidence: administrative centre of the Great Oasis; probable councillors (bouleutai) in the 4th-c. Douch ostraca; a polis in P. Lips. I 64 (368/9); houses of a Hellenized elite at Ain Turba (late 3rd-4th c.) with Greek ostraca and a school tablet with Iliad phrases beside Coptic letters; Greek graffiti at Bagawat naming the 'polis of Hibis' (7th-8th c.)
status_evidence: metropolis of the Great Oasis; bouleutai late 3rd-4th c. (Douch ostraca, as interpreted by Bagnall & Tallet 2015); polis in P. Lips. I 64 (368/9); see of the Great Oasis (Oasis Magna) in Thebaid I in the later lists of sees
note: The Samians of Hdt. 3.26 are often taken as Greek traders settled in the oasis under Amasis; nothing else is known of them. Bagnall and Tallet (2019) stress how little is known of the administration of the oasis. The ancient town lies largely under fields. The Demotic ostraca of the Persian period from Ayn Manawir in the same oasis (5th-4th c. BC; Chauveau) show an Egyptian-speaking farming community and no Greek settlers, which supports not opening a Greek phase in 525 BC.
sources: Hdt. 3.26; Bagnall & Tallet, ZPE 196 (2015); Bagnall & Tallet (eds.), The Great Oasis of Egypt (2019); Evagrius, HE 1.7; Wagner, Les oasis d'Egypte (1987)

list_group: Red Sea coast and the oases
other_names: Mothiton polis ('city of the Mothites'); Mathon
site: Mut el-Kharab, on the edge of Mut, Dakhla Oasis, New Valley Governorate
greek_from_text: 'the city of the Mothites' in Greek contracts from Kellis of c. 299 (SB XXIV 15901, restored) and 320 (P. Kell. I Gr. 52); capital of the Mothite nome, probably created about then; listed as a polis beside Hibis and Trimithis in P. Lips. I 64 (368/9)
until_text: Pottery and a church show the town in use to the 6th-7th c. and later (Fatimid and Mamluk pottery). No Greek texts of residents later than the 4th-5th c. have been published, but documentation from the oasis is thin after c. 400, so the silence is not evidence of an early end. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: 4th-c. Greek and Coptic papyri of the Mothite nome (Kellis); church and pottery to the 6th-7th c. (Dakhleh Oasis Project). Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
ended_by: No named act: the town lived on, and Greek gave way to Coptic and then Arabic after the Arab conquest of Egypt (641). Under Arab rule the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers kept in Arabic from 705/706 (al-Kindi); this ended Greek as the language of government, and no ban on Greek speech is recorded.
pre_greek_note: The Dakhleh Oasis Project gives the Egyptian name as Mt/Mrt; Trismegistos and the 4CARE gazetteer give Pa-Mwt (with a query in Trismegistos).
bilingual_evidence: capital of the Mothite nome and a polis from c. 299 (Kellis contracts; P. Lips. I 64, 368/9); seat of a bishop in the 4th c.; Greek and Coptic documents from the nome (Kellis papyri) show a Greek-writing local elite tied to the city
status_evidence: metropolis of the Mothite nome; polis in SB XXIV 15901 (c. 299), P. Kell. I Gr. 52 (320) and P. Lips. I 64 (368/9); bishop's seat in the 4th c.; Trismegistos Places 3154
note: Most Greek evidence for the Mothite nome comes from the village of Kellis; the city itself is little excavated, and the date of the Mothite nome is not certain (Bagnall and Tallet 2019 warn that the administration of the oasis is poorly known).
sources: Hope, Mut el-Kharab (Dakhleh Oasis Project); P. Lips. I 64; Bagnall & Tallet (eds.), The Great Oasis of Egypt (2019); Trismegistos Geo 3154

list_group: Red Sea coast and the oases
period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
other_names: Mus Hormos; the site was reoccupied as the medieval port of Quseir al-Qadim (Arabic)
site: Quseir al-Qadim, 8 km north of El-Quseir, Red Sea Governorate
greek_from_text: Ptolemaic harbour, first named by Agatharchides (mid-2nd c. BC; Diod. 3.39); a foundation under Ptolemy II is often assumed, but the excavations found little Ptolemaic material; the Roman port town flourished from the late 1st c. BC
until_text: The Roman harbour silted and the town was given up; the excavators date the end of Roman occupation to the 3rd c., with the harbour largely disused by the mid-2nd c. The site was reoccupied only as the Islamic port of Quseir al-Qadim (12th-15th c.).
fade_evidence: Greek ostraca and papyri of the 1st-2nd c. AD (letters, accounts, customs passes) beside Latin, South Arabian, Tamil and Nabataean texts; no Roman occupation layers after the 3rd c.
ended_by: No named act: abandoned as the harbour silted and the trade moved to Berenike and Klysma (excavators' view).
status_evidence: Ptolemaic and Roman port town (Strabo 16.4.24, 17.1.45; Periplus 1, 19); identified by Peacock and Blue's excavations; Greek ostraca and papyri of residents; no civic institutions attested
note: A port town of traders, soldiers and officials with no attested civic institutions; included as a Ptolemaic port settlement with Greek-speaking residents, as Cohen and Mueller treat it.
sources: Strabo 17.1.45; Periplus Maris Erythraei 1, 19; Peacock & Blue, Myos Hormos - Quseir al-Qadim (2006, 2011); Cohen 2006; Wikipedia: Myos Hormos

list_group: Red Sea coast and the oases
period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
site: unlocated; Red Sea coast between the Gulf of Suez and Quseir (Mersa Gawasis and the Safaga area have been proposed), Red Sea Governorate
greek_from_text: founded under Ptolemy II by his officer Satyros and named after the king's sister Philotera, c. 270 BC (Strabo 16.4.5, after Artemidorus; Pithom stele)
until_text: Nothing is known of the town after its foundation; Strabo's source (c. 100 BC) still names it and Ptolemy's Geography (mid-2nd c. AD) lists only a harbour of that name. No remains have been identified.
fade_evidence: last named by Ptolemy, Geog. 4.5 (mid-2nd c. AD), as a harbour
ended_by: No named act: the place is unlocated and simply drops out of the sources.
status_evidence: royal foundation of Ptolemy II (Strabo 16.4.5); Cohen 2006 (Red Sea foundations)
note: Included as a named royal foundation; no town remains or Greek documents of residents are known, and it may never have been more than a harbour settlement.
sources: Strabo 16.4.5; Ptolemy, Geog. 4.5; Cohen 2006; Mueller 2006

list_group: Red Sea coast and the oases
other_names: chief place of the Small Oasis (Oasis Parva); the oasis was later called the 'Oasis of Oxyrhynchus' (Coptic period) and the 'Oasis of el-Bahnasa' (Arabic)
site: El-Qasr, beside El-Bawiti, Bahariya Oasis, Giza Governorate
greek_from_text: Greek dedications from the town, c. AD 1 (SB XXII 15621; SEG LIII 1956); earlier Greek presence in the oasis (Alexander's temple of Ammon at Qasr el-Miqisba; Greco-Roman necropolis at El-Bawiti) does not show a civic community
until_text: Greek ostraca of the oasis run to the early 5th c., a pagarch is attested in the 5th-6th c., and 5th-c. churches carry Greek inscriptions; the later oasis was Coptic-speaking ('Oasis of Oxyrhynchus') and then Arabic. Later Greek evidence is lacking, but so is evidence of any kind. After 641: no evidence either way for Greek speakers in the town, so the end is the Egypt-wide estimate, c. 750 (650-850).
fade_evidence: Greek ostraca dated 374/5-412/3 (era years); Bir Shawish ostraca to 403 and the 5th c.; 5th-c. churches with Greek inscriptions (found 2019-2021). Egypt-wide markers: see the Egypt-wide estimate.
ended_by: No named act: Greek faded in late antiquity and after the Arab conquest of Egypt (641); the oasis later became Muslim. Under Arab rule the governor 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Malik had the registers kept in Arabic from 705/706 (al-Kindi); this ended Greek as the language of government, and no ban on Greek speech is recorded.
pre_greek_note: Egyptian form as given by Trismegistos (with the gloss 'the wall'); no hieroglyphic or Demotic attestation is cited.
bilingual_evidence: called the metropolis of the Small Oasis (Wagner 1987; Trismegistos); Greek dedications from the town of the 1st c. AD (SB XXII 15621; SEG LIII 1956); Greek ostraca of the oasis, 374/5-412/3; 5th-c. churches with Greek inscriptions
status_evidence: metropolis of the Small Oasis according to Wagner 1987 and Trismegistos Places 8248; Greek dedications of the 1st c. AD; no boule, gymnasium or bishop known
note: The Small Oasis was closely tied to the Oxyrhynchite nome, and its civic status is poorly documented; included only on the evidence that Psobthis was the metropolis of the oasis.
sources: Wagner, Les oasis d'Egypte (1987) 197-198; Trismegistos Geo 8248; Bagnall, review of Wagner (BASP); Wikipedia: Bahariya Oasis

list_group: Red Sea coast and the oases
site: Amheida, Dakhla Oasis, New Valley Governorate
greek_from_text: a village that became a polis by 304, when a Greek contract from Kellis names a man 'from the city of the Trimithites' (P. Kell. I Gr. 49); the date of the grant is unknown. The house of the councillor Serenos (c. 340-365), the Greek school and P. Lips. I 64 (368/9) show the city in the mid-4th c.
until_text: The town declined after the 360s (the house of Serenos abandoned c. 365); coins run to the end of the 4th or the early 5th c., when dunes covered the town. It was never reoccupied.
fade_evidence: house B1 (Serenos) abandoned c. 365; coins to the late 4th/early 5th c.; sand invasion at the end of the 4th c. or soon after (Davoli in An Oasis City, 2015)
ended_by: No named act: decline after the 360s and abandonment around 400, as dunes invaded the town and the water supply failed (excavators' view).
bilingual_evidence: a polis by 304 (P. Kell. I Gr. 49) and beside Hibis and Mothis in P. Lips. I 64 (368/9); house of the city councillor Serenos with household records in Greek; a school (mid-4th c.) with Greek verses painted on the walls; Greek ostraca of residents (O. Trim.)
status_evidence: polis in P. Kell. I Gr. 49 (304) and P. Lips. I 64 (368/9); councillor Serenos (O. Trim.); NYU excavations from 2004
note: Kellis, 30 km to the east, has richer Greek papyri but remained a village.
sources: Bagnall et al., An Oasis City (2015); Ast & Bagnall, O. Trim. I (2016); P. Kell. I Gr. 49; P. Lips. I 64

period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
other_names: Leukaspis (Λευκάσπις)? (both names are proposed for the excavated town)
site: Marina El Alamein, Matrouh Governorate
greek_from_text: the excavated town at Marina el-Alamein was founded in the second half of the 2nd c. BC (Polish excavations)
until_text: The town declined after an earthquake in the mid-3rd c. AD and was abandoned at the end of the 6th or beginning of the 7th c.; Greek speech ended with the abandonment.
fade_evidence: Greek public inscriptions for Trajan or Hadrian, for the prefect of Egypt T. Flavius Titianus (129) and for Commodus (182-183); church of c. 400; bishops of Antiphrai Menas (362) and Apollo (458/459); desertion c. 600.
ended_by: No named act: the town shrank after the mid-3rd-c. earthquake (natural) and was deserted c. 600, before the Arab conquest of 642.
status_evidence: forum/agora, civic basilica, baths and Greek public inscriptions; see of Antiphrai (bishops 362, 458/459), if the identification holds
note: The ancient name of the Marina el-Alamein town is not secure (Antiphrai or Leukaspis). The site lies at the western edge of the Mareotis and may also appear among the Egyptian cities.
sources: Daszewski, Marina el-Alamein reports (PCMA); PATHs: Marina el-Alamein; Wikipedia: Diocese of Antiphrae

site: Tobruk, Butnan District
greek_from_text: first named as a harbour of Marmarica in Roman-period sources (Ptolemy; Stadiasmus Maris Magni); a see in late antiquity
until_text: Administration: a harbour town and see of Libya Inferior until 'Amr ibn al-'As's advance through Marmarica, 642. Speech: Greek after the conquest is not attested. There is no evidence either way on how long Greek speakers stayed: no Greek text of a resident is known from after 642, and the Arabic accounts of the conquest of Barqa name only the Lawata Berbers as the party to the treaty (Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam). The end date is that of the conquest, and the range allows for a remnant.
fade_evidence: bishop Serapion at Nicaea, 325; Aemilianus at the council of Constantinople, 553; Justinian made it a garrisoned stronghold against the Moors (Procopius, Buildings 6.2.2); no later Greek evidence.
ended_by: Arab conquest of Marmarica by 'Amr ibn al-'As, 642; no named later act.
status_evidence: Greek name; harbour town; see of Libya Inferior (Serapion at Nicaea 325; Aemilianus 553); stronghold under Justinian
note: Positive evidence of a resident Greek-speaking civic community is thin: a Greek name, a harbour and a see in a province whose hinterland was Libyan.
sources: Ptolemy, Geography 4.5; Stadiasmus Maris Magni; Le Quien, Oriens Christianus II; Wikipedia: Tobruk

site: Susa (Marsa Susa), Jabal al Akhdar District
greek_from_text: harbour of Cyrene from its early years (earliest finds c. 600 BC); an independent city of the Pentapolis from the Hellenistic period (2nd-1st c. BC)
until_text: Administration: seat of the governor of Libya Superior in the 6th c.; Roman rule ended with the Arab conquest, 642/643. Speech: Greek after 643 is not attested; the town seems to have shrunk to little after the conquest. There is no evidence either way on how long Greek speakers stayed after the conquest: no Greek inscription, papyrus or letter of a resident is known from after 643, and the Arabic accounts of the conquest name only the Lawata Berbers as the party to the treaty of Barqa and its tribute (Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam, Futuh Misr), saying nothing of the Greek townspeople. The end date is therefore that of the conquest, and the range allows for a Greek-speaking remnant.
fade_evidence: damage in the earthquake of 365 and subsidence of the harbour (natural); 5th-6th c. churches and the governor's palace with Greek inscriptions; no Greek text after 643. The modern town was founded in 1897 by Muslim refugees from Crete, many Greek-speaking: later newcomers, not a continuation of the ancient community.
ended_by: Arab conquest of the Pentapolis by 'Amr ibn al-'As, 642/643 (Barqa capitulated and agreed a tribute of 13,000 dinars: Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam; al-Baladhuri; al-Bakri); no named later act. Earlier: the earthquake of 365 (natural) and the raids of Synesius' time.
status_evidence: Pentapolis city (Strabo 17.3.20 as harbour of Cyrene; independent city from the Hellenistic period); renamed Sozousa and seat of the governor of Libya Superior; see in late antiquity
note: The move of the governor's seat from Ptolemais is dated to the 5th or 6th c.; one recent study puts it c. 468-470.
sources: Strabo 17.3.20; Laronde 1987; Goodchild 1976; Wikipedia: Apollonia (Cyrenaica)
refoundations: Renamed Sozousa in late antiquity (same site)

site: Wadi el-Khalij, near Bomba on the Gulf of Bomba, Derna District
greek_from_text: the Theraean colonists moved from Platea to Aziris and stayed six years before moving to Cyrene in 631 BC (Hdt. 4.157-158); Greek pottery from c. 640 BC at the site
until_text: Herodotus has the colonists leave for Cyrene after six years; the excavated pottery runs to c. 570 BC, so a small Greek settlement stayed on until then.
fade_evidence: excavated pottery from c. 640 to c. 570 BC.
ended_by: No named act: the colonists moved to Cyrene, guided by Libyans, c. 631 BC (Hdt. 4.158); the remaining settlement was given up c. 570 BC.
status_evidence: seat of the Theraean colony for six years (Hdt. 4.157-158); excavated Greek settlement
note: It housed the whole colonial community before Cyrene, but it was a temporary seat rather than a lasting city.
sources: Hdt. 4.157-158; Boardman, BSA 61 (1966); Laronde 1987

other_names: Barqa (Arabic; capital of the Arab province, whose name passed to all Cyrenaica)
site: old town of Al Marj (destroyed by the 1963 earthquake), Marj District
greek_from_text: founded c. 560-550 BC by brothers of King Arkesilaos II of Cyrene who quarrelled with him (Hdt. 4.160)
until_text: Administration: Barke capitulated to 'Amr ibn al-'As in 642/643 and became Barqa, capital of the Arab province. Speech: Greek after 643 is not attested; Arab writers describe its people as Berbers (Lawata) and Arabs. There is no evidence either way on how long Greek speakers stayed after the conquest: no Greek inscription, papyrus or letter of a resident is known from after 643, and the Arabic accounts of the conquest name only the Lawata Berbers as the party to the treaty of Barqa and its tribute (Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam, Futuh Misr), saying nothing of the Greek townspeople. The end date is therefore that of the conquest, and the range allows for a Greek-speaking remnant.
fade_evidence: sacked by the Persians, 515/514 BC; eclipsed by its harbour Ptolemais from the 3rd c. BC and a small town under Rome; bishops Zopyros (325), Zenobios (431), Theodoros (449); al-Bakri (11th c.) describes Barqa as a prosperous Muslim town exporting wool and honey; decline after the Banu Hilal invasion (11th c.).
ended_by: Capitulated to 'Amr ibn al-'As, 642/643, agreeing a tribute of 13,000 dinars (Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam; al-Baladhuri; al-Bakri). Earlier: besieged and sacked by the Persian satrap Aryandes for Pheretime, 515/514 BC, part of its people deported to Bactria by Darius I (Hdt. 4.200-204). No named act ends Greek speech after 643. Later: c. 688-690 an imperial force landed in Cyrenaica and killed the Arab commander Zuhayr ibn Qays al-Balawi near Barqa, and Barqa was briefly out of Muslim control; no Greek-speaking civil community is attested in connection with it.
founder: brothers of Arkesilaos II of Cyrene
pre_greek_note: Herodotus says the founders won over the local Libyans (4.160); no earlier town is known at the site.
status_evidence: IACP 1025; coinage of the 5th-4th c. BC; see (bishops at Nicaea 325, Ephesus 431 and 449)
note: Barke lay inland; its harbour became Ptolemais (separate entry). No ancient remains are visible at Al Marj.
sources: Hdt. 4.160, 4.200-204; IACP 1025; Laronde 1987; Wikipedia: Barca (ancient city)

period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
site: Sidi Khrebish, Benghazi, Benghazi District
greek_from_text: founded c. 250-246 BC beside Euesperides and named after Berenike II, daughter of Magas and wife of Ptolemy III
until_text: Administration: Roman rule ended with the Arab conquest, 642/643. Speech: the Sidi Khrebish quarter was occupied into the 7th c.; Greek after 643 is not attested. Medieval Barniq was a small place; the modern name Benghazi comes from a local saint. There is no evidence either way on how long Greek speakers stayed after the conquest: no Greek inscription, papyrus or letter of a resident is known from after 643, and the Arabic accounts of the conquest name only the Lawata Berbers as the party to the treaty of Barqa and its tribute (Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam, Futuh Misr), saying nothing of the Greek townspeople. The end date is therefore that of the conquest, and the range allows for a Greek-speaking remnant.
fade_evidence: Greek decrees of the Jewish politeuma (1st c. BC-1st c. AD); bishop Dachius at Nicaea, 325; Justinian rebuilt the circuit wall and built a public bath (Procopius, Buildings 6.2.5); no Greek text after 643.
ended_by: Arab conquest of the Pentapolis by 'Amr ibn al-'As, 642/643 (Barqa capitulated and agreed a tribute of 13,000 dinars: Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam; al-Baladhuri; al-Bakri); no named later act.
founder: a Ptolemaic ruler, traditionally Ptolemy III (named for Berenike II)
status_evidence: Pentapolis city; Greek civic and Jewish politeuma decrees; see (Dachius at Nicaea 325)
note: The founder is disputed: some credit Berenike II herself, in the years after Magas' death, rather than Ptolemy III.
sources: Cohen 2006; Lloyd (ed.), Excavations at Sidi Khrebish, Benghazi (Berenice); Procopius, Buildings 6.2; Reynolds 1977

other_names: Claudiopolis (briefly, after the earthquake of 262, honouring Claudius II); Grennah (local Arabic form recorded by 19th-c. travellers); Qurina (modern Arabic name of the ruins)
site: Shahhat, Jabal al Akhdar District
greek_from_text: founded by Theraean colonists under Battos I (Aristoteles), 631 BC by the traditional date (Hdt. 4.150-159; Pindar, Pythian 4-5); the earliest Greek pottery at the site is of the late 7th c. BC
until_text: Administration: Roman rule ended with the Arab conquest of the Pentapolis, 642/643. Speech: Greek was the language of the shrunken late-antique town (Greek inscriptions of the 5th-6th c.); no Greek text of residents after 643 is known, and how long a Greek-speaking remnant stayed is unknown. There is no evidence either way on how long Greek speakers stayed after the conquest: no Greek inscription, papyrus or letter of a resident is known from after 643, and the Arabic accounts of the conquest name only the Lawata Berbers as the party to the treaty of Barqa and its tribute (Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam, Futuh Misr), saying nothing of the Greek townspeople. The end date is therefore that of the conquest, and the range allows for a Greek-speaking remnant.
fade_evidence: Jewish revolt of 115-117: temples of Apollo and Zeus, the Caesareum and roads destroyed (Dio 68.32; Euseb. HE 4.2), rebuilt under Hadrian; earthquake of 262 and the great earthquake of 21 July 365 (natural); seat of government moved to Ptolemais c. 300; Synesius (c. 400-413) describes a poor, half-empty city and raids by the Ausurians (Austuriani) in 405 and 411-412; the inhabited area shrank in the 5th-6th c., but the Central and East churches were built then and bishops are known to Leontius (c. 600); no Greek text after 643.
ended_by: Arab conquest of the Pentapolis by 'Amr ibn al-'As, 642/643 (Barqa capitulated and agreed a tribute of 13,000 dinars: Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam; al-Baladhuri; al-Bakri). Earlier blows: the Jewish revolt of 115-117 under Lukuas (Andreas), the Marmaritae raid repulsed in 268/269, the raids of the Ausurians (Austuriani) and Macetae described by Synesius (405, 411-412), and the earthquakes of 262 and 365 (natural events). No named act ends Greek speech after 643.
pre_greek_note: Herodotus says Libyans led the settlers to the spring of Apollo (4.158); no pre-Greek town is known at the site.
status_evidence: IACP 1028; civic coinage from the 6th c. BC; boule, demos, gymnasium and ephebes; Pentapolis city; see in late antiquity
note: The colonists' earlier seats at Platea and Aziris are separate entries.
sources: Hdt. 4.150-159; IACP 1028; Laronde 1987; Synesius, Catastasis and Letters; Dio 68.32; Euseb. HE 4.2
refoundations: Restored by Hadrian after the revolt of 115-117 (same site); briefly Claudiopolis after 262

site: Derna, Derna District
greek_from_text: first named in Roman-period geography (Ptolemy, 2nd c. AD) as a town at the eastern edge of the Pentapolis; a Greek see by the 4th c.
until_text: Administration: civil and later church metropolis of Libya Inferior; Roman rule ended with the Arab conquest, 642/643. Speech: Greek after the conquest is not attested. There is no evidence either way on how long Greek speakers stayed after the conquest: no Greek inscription, papyrus or letter of a resident is known from after 643, and the Arabic accounts of the conquest name only the Lawata Berbers as the party to the treaty of Barqa and its tribute (Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam, Futuh Misr), saying nothing of the Greek townspeople. The end date is therefore that of the conquest, and the range allows for a Greek-speaking remnant.
fade_evidence: bishops Piso (347), Dioscurus (c. 410, in a dispute with Paul of Erythron settled by Synesius, Ep. 67), Daniel (431), Theodore (5th c., John Moschus); no Greek evidence after 643.
ended_by: Arab conquest of the Pentapolis by 'Amr ibn al-'As, 642/643 (Barqa capitulated and agreed a tribute of 13,000 dinars: Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam; al-Baladhuri; al-Bakri); no named later act. Later: in 688 raiders from the imperial forces killed the Arab commander Zuhayr ibn Qays al-Balawi and some seventy of his men in the province of Barqa; he is buried at Derna (the Sahaba mosque). This was a military raid and brought back no Greek-speaking community.
pre_greek_note: The name Darnis is not Greek and may be Libyan, but it is known only from Greek and Latin sources.
status_evidence: see from the 4th c. (Piso 347; Daniel at Ephesus 431); metropolis of Libya Inferior
note: Its Greek character rests on the see, Synesius' letters and its place on the Pentapolis coast; its Hellenistic history is unknown. Ptolemy and Ammianus place it in the Pentapolis, later lists in Libya Inferior.
sources: Ptolemy, Geography 4.4; Synesius, Ep. 67; Le Quien, Oriens Christianus II; Wikipedia: Derna, Libya

period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
site: Al Athrun (Latrun), 9 km east of Ras al-Hilal, Derna District
greek_from_text: a Hellenistic foundation on the coast east of Apollonia: occupation from the 4th c. BC (French excavations); named by Ptolemy (Geography 4.4.3); a see from the second half of the 4th c. AD
until_text: Administration: Roman rule ended with the Arab conquest, 642/643. Speech: the town was occupied until the 8th c., but Greek after 643 is not attested. There is no evidence either way on how long Greek speakers stayed after the conquest: no Greek inscription, papyrus or letter of a resident is known from after 643, and the Arabic accounts of the conquest name only the Lawata Berbers as the party to the treaty of Barqa and its tribute (Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam, Futuh Misr), saying nothing of the Greek townspeople. The end date is therefore that of the conquest, and the range allows for a Greek-speaking remnant.
fade_evidence: see from the later 4th c.; bishop Paul (c. 410, Synesius, Ep. 67); a cathedral with baptistery and a pilgrimage church of the 6th c.; occupation to the 8th c.; no Greek text after 643.
ended_by: Arab conquest of the Pentapolis by 'Amr ibn al-'As, 642/643 (Barqa capitulated and agreed a tribute of 13,000 dinars: Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam; al-Baladhuri; al-Bakri); no named later act.
status_evidence: see from the later 4th c. (Paul, c. 410: Synesius, Ep. 67); greatest extent in late antiquity; 6th-c. cathedral and pilgrimage church
note: A village or large town under the early Empire; its rise to a city came with the see. Synesius shows its diocese reaching over the villages of Hydrax and Palaebisca.
sources: Synesius, Ep. 67; Ptolemy, Geography 4.4.3; Widrig, PBSR 46 (1978); French mission: Erythron (Latrun)

site: Sidi Abeid, Benghazi, Benghazi District
greek_from_text: the earliest Greek pottery from the Sidi Abeid excavations is usually put in the early 6th c. BC, though its dating is disputed; Herodotus names the city in the events of 515 BC (4.171, 4.204)
until_text: Abandoned c. 250 BC when its people moved to the new city of Berenike nearby (latest coins of the 250s BC); Greek speech went on at Berenike.
fade_evidence: new settlers sent by Arkesilaos IV c. 462 BC; besieged by Libyans and relieved by Gylippos' Peloponnesian ships in 413 BC (Thuc. 7.50.2); last coins c. 250 BC.
ended_by: No named act: the city was given up c. 250 BC and its people moved to Berenike, named after Berenike II; silting of the harbour lagoon and Ptolemaic policy after the reconquest of Cyrenaica are the usual explanations.
status_evidence: IACP 1026; coinage of the 5th-4th c. BC; Thuc. 7.50.2; Hdt. 4.171, 4.204
note: Euesperides and Berenike are separate sites within Benghazi; the mother city is not recorded and Cyrene is assumed. Some accounts date the foundation as late as c. 525 BC; the city is certainly older than 515 BC.
sources: IACP 1026; Thuc. 7.50.2; Hdt. 4.171, 4.204; Wilson et al., Libyan Studies (Euesperides reports); Cohen 2006
refoundations: Euesperides -> Berenike (c. 250-246 BC; new site, separate entry)

site: Daryanah (Driana), Benghazi District
greek_from_text: founded by Hadrian (117-138), probably soon after the Jewish revolt, when he sent settlers to the devastated province (Orosius 7.12.6)
until_text: Named in the Antonine Itinerary, the Peutinger Table and the Ravenna Cosmography; its later history and the date it was deserted are unknown.
fade_evidence: no inscriptions, bishops or late-antique texts of the town are known.
ended_by: No named act is recorded for the town; the Pentapolis fell to 'Amr ibn al-'As in 642/643.
status_evidence: imperial foundation bearing Hadrian's name, on the Peutinger Table (with town vignette) and in the Antonine Itinerary
note: The settlers' origin and language are not recorded; Greek is assumed from the Pentapolis setting without direct evidence from the site, which may lie at Wadi Jawbiyah rather than Daryanah.
sources: Orosius 7.12.6; Tabula Peutingeriana 7C4; Barrington Atlas 38 B1; Pleiades 373824

site: Qasr Libya, between Al Marj and Al Bayda, Jabal al Akhdar District
greek_from_text: named in Roman-period geography (Ptolemy); a see by c. 410 (Synesius)
until_text: Administration: refounded by Justinian as Theodorias in 539; Roman rule ended with the Arab conquest, 642/643. Speech: Greek after 643 is not attested. There is no evidence either way on how long Greek speakers stayed after the conquest: no Greek inscription, papyrus or letter of a resident is known from after 643, and the Arabic accounts of the conquest name only the Lawata Berbers as the party to the treaty of Barqa and its tribute (Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam, Futuh Misr), saying nothing of the Greek townspeople. The end date is therefore that of the conquest, and the range allows for a Greek-speaking remnant.
fade_evidence: bishops Athamas and Antonios (Synesius, c. 412), Publius (431), Makarios and Theodoros (539/540); Greek mosaic inscriptions of the East Church dated 539/540; no Greek text after 643.
ended_by: Arab conquest of the Pentapolis by 'Amr ibn al-'As, 642/643 (Barqa capitulated and agreed a tribute of 13,000 dinars: Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam; al-Baladhuri; al-Bakri). Earlier: damage from raiders in the 5th and early 6th c. before Justinian's refoundation.
status_evidence: see from c. 410 (Synesius); refounded as a 'new city' (polis nea) Theodorias by Justinian, 539 (dated mosaics)
note: The identification of Qasr Libya with Olbia rests on the mosaics and the episcopal list.
sources: Synesius, Letters; Alfoldi-Rosenbaum & Ward-Perkins 1980; Livius: Theodorias; Wikipedia: Olbia, Libya

period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
site: Marsa Matruh, Matrouh Governorate
greek_from_text: Alexander passed it on his way to Siwa in 331 BC (Arrian, Anabasis 3.3.3); a Ptolemaic harbour and naval base from the 3rd c. BC
until_text: Administration: metropolis of Libya Inferior; taken in 'Amr ibn al-'As's advance west in 642; al-Baratun was then a station on the Arab coastal road. Speech: Greek after the conquest is not attested.
fade_evidence: bishops Titus (Nicaea 325) and Gaius (Alexandria 362); Justinian made it a garrisoned stronghold against the Moors (Procopius, Buildings 6.2.2); no Greek document of residents after 642.
ended_by: Taken by 'Amr ibn al-'As on his march to Barqa, 642; no named later act. Earlier: Cornelius Gallus seized the town for Octavian and beat off Antony's attack, 30 BC (Dio 51.9), without ending it.
pre_greek_note: A Late Bronze Age trading post on Bates's Island in the lagoon (14th-13th c. BC) had Cypriot and Aegean pottery but was not a Greek settlement and has no link with the later town.
status_evidence: Strabo 17.1.14 (city and large harbour); see (Titus at Nicaea 325); metropolis of Libya Inferior; Justinian's stronghold
note: No ancient source records a royal foundation; a foundation by Alexander or the first Ptolemies is sometimes suggested.
sources: Strabo 17.1.14; Arrian, Anabasis 3.3.3; Procopius, Buildings 6.2; White, Marsa Matruh (2002); Wikipedia: Marsa Matruh

other_names: harbour of Barke before the refoundation; Tulmaytha (Arabic)
site: Tolmeita, Marj District
greek_from_text: small Greek harbour settlement from the late 7th or early 6th c. BC (archaeology), later the port of Barke ('the harbour of the Barkaians' in Pseudo-Scylax 108, 4th c. BC); refounded on the same site as the city of Ptolemais under the Ptolemies in the 3rd c. BC (Ptolemy III is usually named, though Ptolemy I has been proposed; its citizens are attested by c. 250 BC)
until_text: Administration: capital of Libya Superior from c. 300; Roman rule ended with the Arab conquest, 642/643. Speech: occupation went on for centuries (glazed wares of the 10th-13th c.), but Greek after 643 is not attested. There is no evidence either way on how long Greek speakers stayed after the conquest: no Greek inscription, papyrus or letter of a resident is known from after 643, and the Arabic accounts of the conquest name only the Lawata Berbers as the party to the treaty of Barqa and its tribute (Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam, Futuh Misr), saying nothing of the Greek townspeople. The end date is therefore that of the conquest, and the range allows for a Greek-speaking remnant.
fade_evidence: Synesius, bishop here c. 410-413, describes raids by the Ausurians (Austuriani) and the town under siege; the edict of Anastasius on the Libyan garrison (c. 501) was set up here; Justinian restored the aqueduct of a town half-deserted for lack of water (Procopius, Buildings 6.2.9-11); domestic occupation into the Islamic period (Ward-Perkins; Kennet 1991); no Greek text after 643.
ended_by: Arab conquest of the Pentapolis by 'Amr ibn al-'As, 642/643 (Barqa capitulated and agreed a tribute of 13,000 dinars: Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam; al-Baladhuri; al-Bakri). Earlier: the raids of the Ausurians (Austuriani) described by Synesius (405, 411-412) and the earthquake of 365 (natural). No named act ends Greek speech after 643.
founder: Barke (as its harbour); refounded as Ptolemais by a Ptolemaic king (Ptolemy I, II or III; disputed)
pre_greek_note: Before the refoundation the site was the Greek harbour of Barke; no pre-Greek settlement is known.
status_evidence: Pentapolis city; Greek civic inscriptions (gymnasiarchs, ephebes); metropolis of Libya Superior; see (Secundus at Nicaea 325, Synesius c. 410-413, Evoptius 431, Georgius 553)
note: The founder is disputed: a papyrus attesting citizens of Ptolemais by 252 BC rules out a foundation by Ptolemy III. Some accounts have the town destroyed and abandoned at the conquest; excavated pottery shows occupation into the Islamic period.
sources: Cohen 2006; Kraeling 1962; Libyan Studies: 'Dating the Ptolemaic city-foundations in Cyrenaica'; Procopius, Buildings 6.2; Kennet 1991
refoundations: Harbour of Barke -> Ptolemais (royal refoundation, mid-3rd c. BC; first papyrus naming its citizens 252 BC; same site)

other_names: Arsinoe (Ἀρσινόη, Ptolemaic name after Arsinoe II); Teucheira (late-antique spelling); Tukra (Arabic)
site: Tocra, Marj District
greek_from_text: the earliest Greek pottery from the sanctuary deposit is of c. 620 BC (Boardman and Hayes); Herodotus (4.171) knows it as a city in the territory of Barke
until_text: Administration: the Arab advance of 642/643 ended Roman rule; the date and manner of Teucheira's own surrender are not recorded. A modern reconstruction (Goodchild) makes Teucheira, which Justinian had strongly fortified, the last stronghold of the Roman forces, from which the garrison and the wealthier townspeople left by sea; the primary source for this evacuation is not securely identified and it should be treated as a hypothesis. Speech: the town lived on under Muslim rule to about the 10th c. (Arabic inscription in the bath), but there is no evidence either way on how long Greek speakers stayed: no Greek text of a resident is known from after 643, and al-Idrisi (12th c.) calls its people Berbers. The end date is that of the conquest, and the range allows for a remnant.
fade_evidence: walls of the late 5th-6th c.; Procopius says Justinian strongly fortified Teucheira (Buildings 6.2.4); Greek inscriptions to the 6th c.; the evacuation of the garrison and the wealthy by sea after 642/643 is a modern reconstruction (Goodchild); Arabic inscription over the door of the bath (King 1989); al-Idrisi: Berber inhabitants.
ended_by: Arab conquest of the Pentapolis by 'Amr ibn al-'As, 642/643 (Barqa capitulated and agreed a tribute of 13,000 dinars: Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam; al-Baladhuri; al-Bakri). Goodchild put the town's fall in a later campaign, with the Roman forces and wealthy townspeople leaving by sea; the sources do not say how it fell. No named act ends Greek speech after 643.
pre_greek_note: The name Taucheira is not Greek and may be Libyan, but it is known only from Greek and Latin sources.
status_evidence: IACP 1029; Pentapolis city; see in late antiquity
note: Recent work dates the walled compound once called the last monument of Roman rule to Anastasius rather than the 640s.
sources: Hdt. 4.171; IACP 1029; Boardman & Hayes, Excavations at Tocra (1966, 1973); Christides 2000; Kenrick 2013
refoundations: Renamed Arsinoe in the 3rd c. BC (same site), later Teucheira again

site: near the mouth of Wadi Ka'am (Wadi Qaam, the ancient Cinyps river) between Al-Khums (Lepcis Magna) and Zliten, Murqub District; exact site unknown
greek_from_text: colony founded on the Cinyps river by the Spartan prince Dorieus, son of King Anaxandridas, with Theraean guides (Hdt. 5.42); the date c. 515/514 BC is a modern reckoning from the accession of Cleomenes I; no archaeological trace of the settlement
until_text: Speech and administration ended together: Herodotus says Dorieus settled 'the fairest spot in Libya, by the river', and was driven out in the third year; the colonists went back to the Peloponnese, and Dorieus later tried again in western Sicily (Herakleia near Eryx), where he was killed (Hdt. 5.42-46).
fade_evidence: Hdt. 5.42 is the only evidence; rescue excavations in the Wadi Ka'am valley found a Punic and Roman cemetery (3rd c. BC - 1st c. AD) but nothing of the Spartan settlement.
ended_by: Expelled in the third year by the Macae, other Libyans and the Carthaginians (Hdt. 5.42), c. 512 BC.
founder: Dorieus of Sparta, son of Anaxandridas, with Theraean guides
pre_greek_note: Cinyps (Κίνυψ) is the name of the river and of the Libyan district (Hdt. 4.175, 4.198); no non-Greek form is attested.
status_evidence: Hdt. 5.42 (an organized colony under an oikist, sent out with Theraean guides); not an attested polis with known institutions
note: A real but very short-lived colony (two to three years). Whether it ever functioned as a city with civic institutions is unknown, and it has not been located; it is kept as the only historical Greek foundation in Tripolitania.
sources: Hdt. 5.42-46; Hdt. 4.175, 4.198; Pleiades 344413 (Kinyps, near the mouth of Wadi Caam); Livius: Cinyps (Wadi Qaam); Wikipedia: Dorieus

period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
other_names: Cirta Regia (royal seat of the Numidian kings); colonia Iulia Iuvenalis Honoris et Virtutis Cirta (Roman colony); Constantina (renamed by Constantine, 313); Qusantina (Arabic)
site: Constantine (the Rhumel rock and the El Hofra sanctuary), Constantine Province
greek_from_text: Greek settlers placed in the town by Micipsa, king of Numidia 148-118 BC (Strabo 17.3.13); Greek dedications at the El Hofra sanctuary of Baal Hammon, before the Roman conquest (2nd-1st c. BC)
until_text: Administration: Numidian kings to 46 BC, then Rome. Speech: the Greek community is known only from Strabo's notice on Micipsa and the undated Greek stelae of El Hofra (the dated stelae run from 163/2 to c. 122/1 BC). In 112 BC Jugurtha took Cirta after a long siege and killed Adherbal, the adult Numidians and the foreign traders (Sall. Jug. 26.3); in 46 BC Caesar gave the town to P. Sittius and his men, and Roman Cirta, head of the four colonies, has a large and almost entirely Latin epigraphy. No Greek-speaking community is attested after the 2nd c. BC; the end date is an estimate.
fade_evidence: Last datable El Hofra stelae c. 122/1 BC (Micipsa); Greek stelae individually undated; the Roman colony's inscriptions (CIL VIII, ILAlg II) are Latin.
ended_by: No named act against the Greeks as such: Jugurtha took Cirta in 112 BC and massacred the adult Numidians and the negotiatores (Sall. Jug. 26.3), and Caesar handed the town to P. Sittius and his followers as a Roman colony in 46 BC (App. BC 4.54); whether the Greeks settled by Micipsa were among Jugurtha's victims is not recorded.
founder: Micipsa, king of Numidia, settled Greeks in the existing royal town
pre_greek_note: Cirta was the capital of Syphax and Masinissa before Micipsa (Livy 30.12); the name is native (Libyan or Punic) and is used in Greek and Latin without change; its Punic spelling is not given here.
other_language: Punic (the written and court language of Numidian Cirta) and Libyan (Numidian)
bilingual_evidence: FOR: Strabo 17.3.13 says King Micipsa 'settled a colony of Greeks in it' and made Cirta strong enough to send out 10,000 horse and twice as many foot; among the c. 700 stelae from the El Hofra sanctuary, 17 are inscribed in Greek beside c. 281 Punic and neo-Punic and 7 Latin, so Greek is the second language of the sanctuary (Greek and Latin stelae to Kronos and Tanit, before the Roman conquest: Le Glay 1966); modern accounts describe Micipsa's rebuilt Cirta as a mixed Libyan, Punic and Greek town, with Greek architects at court and refugees, including Greek mercenaries, after the fall of Carthage in 146 BC. AGAINST: no Greek civic institutions or coins; at least one Greek-script stele merely transliterates a Punic text, so some Greek writing comes from Punic speakers; the foreign traders who defended Cirta in 112 BC are called Italici (Sall. Jug. 21, 26).
status_evidence: royal capital of the Numidian kings; Strabo 17.3.13 (Greek settlers); El Hofra Greek stelae (Berthier and Charlier 1955); later Roman colony and see
note: Doubtful case. Strabo's notice is explicit and the El Hofra Greek share (c. 6% of the legible stelae) resembles Rome's, but it rests on one sanctuary and some Greek-script dedicants were Punic speakers; it is kept as the only North African town west of Cyrenaica with a recorded settlement of Greek residents.
sources: Strabo 17.3.13; Sall. Jug. 21-26; Berthier and Charlier, Le sanctuaire punique d'El-Hofra a Constantine (1955); Le Glay, Saturne africain. Monuments II (1966); Wikipedia: Cirta steles
refoundations: Roman colony of P. Sittius, 46 BC; renamed Constantina by Constantine, 313 (same site)

period: 2 The Ptolemies and the kings (332-30 BC)
other_names: Ptolemais of the Hunts; Ptolemais Epitheras (Pliny 6.171); Ptolemais in Troglodytis (Pliny 2.183)
site: unlocated; most likely at Aqiq (Khor Aqiq), Red Sea State, Sudan; Trinkitat, Suakin (Sudan) and Arqiqo (Eritrea) have also been proposed
greek_from_text: founded for Ptolemy II by Eumedes, whom the king sent to the elephant-hunting grounds: he enclosed a peninsula with a ditch and a wall and won over the natives who tried to stop him (Strabo 16.4.7); the Pithom stele (l. 22-24), under year 16 (270/269 BC), records 'a great city' with the king's name built by the general who caught elephants for him, usually taken as this foundation
until_text: Founded as the base of the royal elephant hunt. Administration: the hunts were run by royal commanders and soldiers under Ptolemy II-IV; they were cut off by the Great Revolt of the Thebaid (205-186 BC), which closed the Koptos-Berenike route, and ended in the 2nd c. BC, at the latest when Ptolemy VI's revived programme stopped at his death in 145 (Burstein). Speech: no Greek residents are attested after the hunting period. By c. AD 40-70 the Periplus (ch. 3) knows it only as a small trading place without a harbour, reached by small boats, selling tortoiseshell and a little ivory, on a coast under Zoskales, king of the Aksumites (ch. 5); Greek traders who came by sea from Egypt were visitors, not residents. The end date is an estimate.
fade_evidence: Pithom stele, year 16 (270/269 BC); dedications by the commanders of Ptolemy IV's elephant hunts found in Egypt (OGIS 82-86); noon-shadow observations at Ptolemais reported by Eratosthenes and Pliny (NH 2.183); Agatharchides (c. 145-132 BC) on the hunting coast; Periplus 3 (c. AD 40-70): a small trading place; Ptolemy, Geography 4.7.7 (c. AD 150) still lists it.
ended_by: No named act: the elephant hunts for which the town was founded were cut off by the Great Revolt of the Thebaid under the native pharaohs Haronnophris and Chaonnophris (205-186 BC) and given up by the Ptolemies in the 2nd c. BC, at the latest after the death of Ptolemy VI (145 BC); by the 1st c. AD the coast lay under Zoskales, king of the Aksumites (Periplus 5).
pre_greek_note: Strabo says Eumedes built on a peninsula and won over local people who resisted; no earlier settlement or native name is attested.
status_evidence: royal foundation: 'a city founded by Eumedes' (Strabo 16.4.7); Pithom stele l. 23, 'a great city with the name of the king'; 'oppidum' in Pliny, NH 6.171; listed by Ptolemy, Geography 4.7.7; Cohen 2006
note: The site is not securely located: Aqiq is favoured by Burstein and a Russian-Sudanese survey of 2025 found 3rd-c. BC pottery there, but the identification is unproven. The foundation is well attested, but whether a Greek civic community lived there beyond the king's hunters and soldiers is not documented.
sources: Strabo 16.4.7; Pliny, NH 2.183, 6.171; Pithom stele, l. 22-24 (year 16 of Ptolemy II); Periplus Maris Erythraei 3, 5; Cohen 2006; Mueller 2006; Burstein 2021; Cobb, Greece & Rome 2016
